1. Why is email marketing notable?Email is the marketing tool that helps you  create a seamless, connected, frictionless buyer journey. More importantly, email marketing allows you to build relationships with prospects, customers, and past customers. It's your chance to speak  to them right in their inbox, at a time that suits them. Along with the right message, email can become one of your most powerful marketing channels.2. What is benefits of email marketing?Email marketing is best way for creating long term relationship with your clients, and increasing sales in our tech giant.Benefits of email marketing for bussiness:Better brand recognitionStatistics of what works bestMore salesTargeted audienceMore traffic to your products/services/newsletterBuild credibilityMost  bussinesses are using email marketing and making tons of money with email marketing.3. What is the simplest day and time to send my marketing emails?Again, the answer to this question varies from company to company. And again, testing is the way to find out what works best. Typically, weekends and mornings seem to be  times when multiple emails are opened, but since your audience may have different habits, it's best to experiment and then use your  data to decide. 4. Which metrics should I be looking at?The two most important metrics for email marketing are  open rate and click-through rate. If your emails aren't opened, subscribers will never see your full marketing message, and if they open them but don't click through to your site, your emails won't convert.5. How do I write a decent subject line?The best subject lines are short and to the point, accurately describing  the content of the email, but also catchy and intriguing, so the reader wants to know more. Once Again, this is the perfect place for  A/B testing, to see what types of subject lines work best with your audience. Your call to action should be clear and  simple. It should be somewhere at the top of your email for those who haven't finished reading the entire email,  then repeated  at the end for those reading all the way through. It should state exactly what you want subscribers to do, for example "Click here to download the premium theme for free. 6. Is email marketing still effective?Email marketing is one of the most effective ways for a business to reach its customers directly. Think about it. You don't post something on your site  hoping people will visit it. You don't even post something on a social media page and hope fans  see it. You're sending something straight to each person's inbox, where they'll definitely  see it! Even if they don't open it, they'll still see your subject line and business name every time you send an email, so you're still communicating directly with your audience. 7. However do I grow my email subscribers list? Should i buy an email list or build it myself?Buying an email list is  waste of time & money. These email accounts are unverified and not interested in your brand. The mailing list is useless if your subscribers do not open your emails. There are different ways to grow your mailing list. Give them a free ebook and host it on a landing page where they have to enter the email to download the file and also create a forum page on your website, asks your visitors what questions they might have about your business, and collects email addresses to follow up with them. 8. How do I prevent audience from unsubscribing?If the  subject line of the email is irrelevant to  customers, they will ignore it multiple times. But, if it keeps repeating, they are intercepted and unsubscribed from your emails. So, send relevant emails for the benefit of the customer. Don't send emails that often only focus  on sales, offers and discounts. Submit information about your business and offers so you can connect with customers. You can also enhancement them on recent trends in your industry. The basic role of an email is first and foremost to  connect with customers, get the most out of this tool.9. What is the difference between a cold email and a spam email?Cold emails are mostly sales emails that are sent with content align to the needs of the recipient. It is usually personalized and includes a business perspective. However, it is still an unsolicited email. And all unsolicited emails are marked as SPAM. Regularly receiving this type of unsolicited email in your people' inboxes, chances are  your emails will soon be diverted to  spam or junk folders. The most important thing to prevent this from happening is to respect your recipients' choice to opt-out of receiving emails from you. You can add the links to easily unsubscribe. You must be familiar with the CAN-SPAM Act and its regulations.10. Where can I find email template?Almost all email campaign tools provide you with ready-made templates. Whether you use MailChimp or Pardot, you'll get several email templates ready to use. However, if you want to create a template from scratch, you can do so.Most of email campaign tools have option to paste the HTML code of your own design. 11. What email marketing trend will help marketers succeed in 2022?Is it a trend to listen to  and get to know your customers? I think people realize how bad it feels for a brand or a company to obsess over themselves without knowing their customers personal needs. People who listen empathetically and then provide value based on what they learn will win.Final Saying You can approach email marketing in different ways. We have compiled a list of most frequently asked questions to help you understand how to get started, what constraints you need to keep in mind, and what future development you will need, we don’t have 100% answers to every situation and there’s always a chance you will have something upcoming and different to deal with as you market your own business.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

ROBOTERA disclosed in a November 26, 2026 announcement that 45 of its humanoid robots are being tested for parcel induction at China Post’s Hangzhou Postal District Center.

It has been revealed that china Post’s Hangzhou center officially launched the testing program in April 2026. ROBOTERA describes it as the largest deployment of robots for testing in comparable postal operations nationwide.

In a recent development, parcel induction here covers the handling work that moves packages onto induction platforms within a sorting operation. The robots can independently pick parcels, reorient them, identify and reject irregularly shaped parcels, place parcels onto those platforms, and handle operational exceptions.

That is a broader assignment than a single pick-and-place motion. It combines object recognition, physical manipulation and accept-or-reject decisions with responses to exceptions, giving the fleet several functions within one induction workflow. The testing therefore examines whether humanoids can handle varied parcels and disruptions at a postal facility, rather than only repeat a fixed movement.

ROBOTERA reports that multiple rounds of iterative optimization raised induction efficiency from 500–600 parcels per hour during initial testing to approximately 1,200 parcels per hour during specific testing periods, with operational accuracy above 90% and improvements in motion smoothness, recognition accuracy and handling precision.

In a recent development, those figures describe different aspects of the work: throughput measures speed, while accuracy and handling precision bear on whether parcels are processed correctly. The higher rate applies to particular testing periods, so it represents performance reached during those tests rather than a sustained fleet-wide production average.

It has been revealed that the Hangzhou disclosure follows a separate Guangdong rollout announced on November 17, 2026, which covered 11 postal hubs in eight cities. That project began with a pilot at the Guangzhou Postal District Center in March 2026. ROBOTERA reported an average induction rate above 1,500 parcels per hour there, comparable to the performance of experienced human workers. The rates have different measurement bases: Guangdong’s was an average, while Hangzhou’s higher result came during specific testing periods. The earlier project also spanned a provincial network, whereas Hangzhou concentrates the disclosed fleet at one facility.

Sources indicate that china Post’s Hangzhou branch said it looks to accelerate adoption of automated equipment, including intelligent sorting and security-inspection systems, across more operational scenarios to improve postal-delivery quality and efficiency. That plan would extend automation beyond the induction work covered by the current robot tests.

Hangzhou now provides a concentrated counterpart to the distributed Guangdong project: a single facility where fleet size, multi-step handling and test performance can be assessed together. The branch’s planned expansion into sorting and security inspection broadens the stakes, leaving the operational question of whether the induction results can be maintained as automation covers more of the facility’s workflow.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, apertus 1.5 is a continued pretraining of the first generation model: adding 4 trillion tokens of text and multimodal training data to the 8B model and 2 trillion tokens to the 70B model, for a total of 19T and 17T, respectively.
  • It has been revealed that we introduce multimodality in v1.5 models in an early-fusion manner, where images and audio enter Apertus as discrete tokens in the same sequence with text tokens, instead of using a separate vision encoder.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, our latest release, Apertus 1.5, extends the 8B and 70B Apertus 1.0 models with image/audio understanding, an optional thinking mode, a four times longer context window, improved instruction-following, and better tool use. The updated 8B and 70B model weights were released to Hugging Face on July 24, 2026 under an Apache 2.0 license. Further details are now available from the project Technical Report, and summarized here.

According to recent reports, apertus 1.5 is a continued pretraining of the first generation model: adding 4 trillion tokens of text and multimodal training data to the 8B model and 2 trillion tokens to the 70B model, for a total of 19T and 17T, respectively. As with every Apertus release, the models are fully open: open weights, open data, open values, and full training details.

The full Apertus 1.5 training pipeline.

It has been revealed that we introduce multimodality in v1.5 models in an early-fusion manner, where images and audio enter Apertus as discrete tokens in the same sequence with text tokens, instead of using a separate vision encoder. Images are tokenized with the Emu3.5 tokenizer (a 512×512 image becomes 1,024 tokens) and audio with WavTokenizer (40 tokens per second). We only extend the vocabulary, so the architecture stays unchanged and training runs at text-only speed. The models understand images and audio but generate only text.

Starting from Apertus 1.0, we continue pretraining in four stages:.

Recent findings suggest that overall, more than half of the training tokens are text-only, which preserves the language abilities of Apertus 1.0. The text data is refreshed with sources such as FineWeb2-HQ+, FinePDFs, and Nemotron-CC. All upcoming data, multimodal included, meets the same bar as before: publicly available, permissively licensed, and with robots.txt opt-outs respected retroactively. Every source is listed in apertus-data-transparency.

Post-training runs in five stages: SFT → long-context SFT → RL → DPO → charter alignment (SDPO).

According to recent reports, alongside the extended model capabilities, we also significantly expanded the scope of evaluations. Beyond the existing text-based evaluations used for Apertus 1.0, we added multimodal evaluations (image & audio), and thinking-mode evaluations.

The multimodal evaluations are done through MLLM-eval-suite pipeline, merging two major multimodal evaluation frameworks lmms-eval and VLMEvalKit. We also added a series of text-based benchmarks, as well as extended benchmarking for translation and multilingual capabilities, safety, and tool use. These can be found in our post-training evaluation repository, based on lm-evaluation-harness fork.

It has been revealed that while still trailing frontier open-weight models, the fresh release has also significantly improved performance in coding and instruction following capabilities with Apertus 1.5 8B outperforming similarly sized open-weight models on IF and multilingual tasks. Thinking further improves performance on challenging reasoning-heavy benchmarks like AIME. The multimodal performance of the model is closer to Gemma 4 12B and other current open-weight models. Apertus 1.5 multimodal performance is competitive in spatial understanding among open-weight models and document/chart understanding among open-source models.

Industry observers note that we also thank our collaborators and external evaluators for their help with efficient benchmarking of Apertus capabilities. In particular, Apertus 1.5 reveals strong performance on Swiss Legal tasks, being on par with leading open-weight models (blog, code). Additionally, on Last Translation Benchmark, Apertus 1.5 8B presents machine translation capabilities which match GPT-OSS-20B and outperform models like Claude Haiku 4.5 or Google Translate (leaderboard, paper).

Apertus collaborates with the EvalEval Coalition to ensure fully transparent and reproducible benchmarking. We publish the Apertus 1.5 results in the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema, a shared format that records not only scores, but also who ran the evaluation, how the model was accessed, the generation settings, and how each metric should be interpreted: details that are routinely missing from leaderboards and that often explain why similar-looking scores differ.

According to recent reports, the results are shown in the Eval Card below, which combines the run data with benchmark and model metadata into one interpretable record, and are also available through Hugging Face Community Evals. This is the same infrastructure the UK AI Security Institute uses to publish its evaluations openly. Since our text evaluations run on our public fork of lm-evaluation-harness, which EEE supports with a dedicated converter, anyone can rerun them and compare their numbers against ours under identical settings.

Structured evaluation reporting also matters beyond research. EvalEval has mapped Evaluation Cards to AI governance requirements, including Article 55 of the EU AI Act and the GPAI Code of Practice, and found that the EEE schema can represent 56 of the 60 evaluation-reporting elements these frameworks call for. This fits how we already release Apertus: alongside the models, we publish a Public Summary of Training Content and, voluntarily, a Code of Practice document. Machine-readable evaluation records are a natural next step: making it easier for regulators, deployers, and researchers to find, interpret, and compare the evidence behind a model.

We are committed to promoting reproducible and transparent evaluation through Eval Cards and the EEE schema, and encourage other model developers to report their results in the same way, so that scores can be compared across models and organizations.

All recipes, ablations, and data mixtures are documented in the Technical Report. We aim to popularize open model development by making the v1.5 training process public and accessible. Intermediate checkpoints are hosted in our Apertus 1.5 Hugging Face collection, including the base weights, SFT, RLVR and DPO, as well as our curated training data mixes/custom datasets in Apertus 1.5 datasets collection. Sharing them allows researchers to investigate how each stage changes the model behavior.

The report covers numerous ablations on the effect of post-training data in different stages, where we observed that the multimodal data mixed in together with text data during SFT helps improve across all modalities. We also find that the benefits of multimodal reasoning traces survive the subsequent text-only reinforcement learning: starting from an SFT checkpoint trained with multimodal traces, RL improves mathematics more than when starting from a text-only checkpoint, and the advantage on reasoning tasks persists throughout training.

Proton Lumo and Infomaniak Euria are two widely used apps that have recently integrated Apertus 1.5. These deployments are linked in the Community Showcase among others - see this discussion thread for a preview.

Access to Apertus 1.5 in the form of an API for developers has been revealed by a range of providers, including Swisscom, Infomaniak, Phoeniqs, and other companies listed in our General Availability guide. The report also provides details on how we work with external evaluators to test and prepare the models.

Technical instructions for running the models are in the model cards of the Apertus releases on Hugging Face and in our Quickstart guide.

According to recent reports, thank you for reading this blog post and being part of our community! We just celebrated five million downloads in our Hugging Face analytics 🤗 and are not slowing down. At the recent AI+X Summit in Zurich, our team revealed the roadmap for Apertus 2.0: sparse/MoE architecture, ~600B total parameters, extended training schedule, with agents, mathematics and coding as priorities.

It has been revealed that in summary: we invite you to read our report, download the models, explore the intermediate checkpoints, finetune the weights, and reproduce our evaluations. Questions that are not already covered in our publications or website FAQ are always welcome, and we would also love to hear which topics would be most useful to the community for future deep dives.

If you build with or use Apertus, please fill out the Showcase form, and reach out through the options on our Contact page. We are looking forward to highlighting more work, learning what you are building, and hearing how Apertus can be improved!

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The flagship 708B-A41B uses approximately 41B active parameters per token, compared with roughly 3.8B for the compact 37B-A4B.
  • Both models use a 3:1 mix of Gated DeltaNet layers and multi-head latent attention layers enhanced with DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The GigaChat Team confirmed GigaChat 4 on November 26, 2026, releasing 708B- and 37B-parameter mixture-of-experts models with native one-million-token context windows. Both activate only a subset of their parameters per token, support tool calling and multi-step agent tasks, and allow Instant or Reasoning responses to be selected per request within one checkpoint.

The flagship 708B-A41B uses approximately 41B active parameters per token, compared with roughly 3.8B for the compact 37B-A4B. Both were trained on sequences extending to the full context length for work with long documents, collections of sources and large codebases. This arrangement replaces GigaChat 3.5’s separate instant and reasoning checkpoints.

Both models use a 3:1 mix of Gated DeltaNet layers and multi-head latent attention layers enhanced with DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA). Gated DeltaNet maintains a fixed-size recurrent state, while DSA selects up to 2,048 earlier positions for each query rather than computing attention over the entire sequence. The companion technical report says indexer and selection overhead can outweigh the attention savings at short contexts or small decode batches.

In a recent development, the flagship has 64 decoder layers and 256 routed experts, selecting eight per token together with one shared expert. The compact model has 32 layers and 192 routed experts, using the same combination of eight routed experts and one shared expert.

Sources indicate that for the 708B model, context extension progressed from 32K to 128K tokens before indexer training and joint optimization at the native length. After supervised fine-tuning, specialist models underwent reinforcement learning in mathematics, coding, tool use and multi-turn agent workflows. Multi-teacher on-policy distillation then consolidated their capabilities into one model offering both response modes.

Under the team’s evaluation protocol, the 708B model scored 71.26% on Terminal-Bench 2.0 in Reasoning mode and 60.47% in Instant mode, versus 30.30% and 12.94% respectively for GigaChat 3.5. Its reported Reasoning results also include 80.89% on SWE-bench Verified and 79.55% on BFCL v4, although GLM-5.3 is listed higher at 86.67% on SWE-bench Verified.

The compact model’s reported Reasoning results include 85.00% on LiveCodeBench v6, 70.80% on SWE-bench Verified and 72.00% on BFCL. For the flagship, evaluation combined public runners and scoring code with the team’s own implementations, including seven-hour timeouts for specified agentic benchmarks.

The team’s demonstrations emphasize tasks that chain artifacts and tools: the flagship modified a Mario cartridge’s palette in its binary file and ran the game on a Mac M4, produced an STL vase for 3D printing, and used MCP access to the Cadenza music workstation to compose a track before building an accompanying visualization site.

The flagship model card lists FP8, BF16 and GGUF instruction-tuned variants, along with base and intermediate checkpoints, and releases its instruction-tuned checkpoint under the MIT License. The compact model card lists the same variant categories but uses the Noncommercial License for Individuals 1.0. The detailed technical report currently covers the 708B model; a dedicated report for the 37B model is planned for later.

It has been revealed that both cards document SGLang and vLLM serving, per-request mode selection and OpenAI-compatible tool calling. They recommend Pi for agentic tasks, with Codex CLI and DeepSeek Harness as alternatives for interactive terminal work.

The flagship’s documented FP8 configuration uses two nodes with eight H100 80 GB GPUs each. The compact model’s example uses one H100 80 GB GPU, with approximately 40 GB required for its weights before attention caches, recurrent states and activations.

According to recent reports, gigaChat 4 makes deployment terms part of the model choice alongside benchmark scores: the flagship combines MIT licensing with a two-node example, while the compact model offers a single-GPU path under noncommercial terms. For prospective users, the compact checkpoint’s usage restrictions are therefore as consequential as its lower hardware requirement.

Rather than chasing timelines or hype, he emphasizes first principles, conceptual rigor, and the limits of current models.

Welcome Beam: a 501B open model you can own, customize, and scale

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face!
  • In a recent development, beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases.
  • Industry observers note that beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face! It is the first model from the new US lab, Reflection, and it’s open! It's a mixture-of-experts (MoEs) model with 501B parameters (23B active per token), supports text as input, has a context window of 1M tokens, and is released under the Apache 2.0 license.

In a recent development, beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases. It is for teams that want a frontier-scale model on their own hardware, infrastructure, or cloud, and want to customize it to their own use cases. Beam ships with its own dedicated open source Rust based harness that delivers the best performance from the model.

Industry observers note that beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang. We’ve worked with the Reflection team to bring you inference, SFT (supervised fine tuning), and RL (reinforcement learning) recipes for you to build with this model for your needs. On top of day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM, this post shows you how to run it, how to post-train it, and what we built with it.

Sources indicate that reflection is going to give out $10,000 Hub credits to the best projects that use Beam. All you have to do is make a thing, and share it on the Hub:.

If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build the space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. We’ll collect all the links, select the best, and send out the credits to your Hub accounts.

Beam is a text-only model built for long-context (1M context length) reasoning and agentic work. It is a sparse MoE model, where each token is computed by a small fraction of the network, so it runs at the speed of a much smaller model while keeping the capacity of a large one.

Recent findings suggest that the decoder has 52 layers with a hidden size of 5,120. Most layers use sliding-window attention over the previous 512 tokens; every sixth layer, and the last one, attend to the full context. That gives 43 sliding-window layers and 9 global ones.

Inside the attention block (both layer types).

The two kinds of layers handle position differently. Sliding-window layers use RoPE, since relative position matters most within a short window. Global layers use no positional encoding. Instead, each query is multiplied by a scaler that grows slowly with the number of visible tokens, (1 + (pos + 1) / 2048) ** 0.1. It acts as a temperature: the softmax keeps its precision as the context lengthens instead of flattening out. The implementation calls this scalable-softmax query scaling.

Industry observers note that attention uses grouped-query attention with 48 query heads and 8 key-value heads, with RMSNorm on queries and keys. A learned sigmoid gate, computed from the layer input, scales every channel of every head before the output projection.

It has been revealed that the first 3 layers use a dense SwiGLU MLP. The other 49 replace it with a Mixture-of-Experts block of 256 experts, each a SwiGLU MLP with an intermediate size of 2,560, or about 39M parameters. The experts hold 98.4% of the model's parameters.

Sources indicate that the router follows DeepSeek-V3's group-limited scheme. It scores all 256 experts with a sigmoid, splits them into 8 groups of 32, keeps the 4 best groups (ranked by the sum of each group's top two scores), then picks the top 8 experts inside them. Beam uses the same group sizes as DeepSeek-V3 but no shared expert. Expert outputs are combined with normalized router weights and scaled by 2.5.

Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 23B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of a 501B model but runs at the speed of a 23B one. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores most parameters in 4-bit precision for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, some parameters are kept in BF16 for accuracy. There are also FP8 checkpoints on the hub which are ideal for Hopper and Ampere series chips.

If you want to deploy Beam yourself, check out the vLLM or SGLang recipes below.

According to recent reports, the residual connections are the most distinctive part. A standard transformer adds each sublayer output to the stream with weight 1, so the stream grows with depth.

Beam counts the input embedding as step 1. At step k it adds the sublayer output with weight 1/sqrt(k) and keeps the existing stream with weight sqrt((k-1)/k). The squares of the two weights sum to one, so the stream stays at a constant scale from the first layer to the last. After all 104 additions, every sublayer output and the input embedding carry the same weight in the final hidden state.

It has been revealed that every sublayer is also normalized before and after, and the final logits pass through a tanh softcap at ±30, computed in FP32. The implementation fixes where it computes in FP32: the router, the SwiGLU product, the norms, RoPE, the query scaling and the softcap.

Hybrid attention works well for long contexts. Each layer caches 2 x 8 KV heads x 128 dims = 2,048 values per token. If all 52 layers kept every token, the cache would grow by 208 KiB per token. Only the 9 global layers keep the whole sequence. The 43 sliding-window layers hold a fixed 512-token window each and stop growing. So the cache grows by 36 KiB per token, roughly a sixth of the naive rate.

These numbers are per sequence, in BF16, with the transformers dynamic cache.

Here are the benchmark results across different precision levels, as provided by the Reflection team.

In a recent development, the most practical way to serve the model is serving the NVFP4 checkpoint, which retains most of the quality of the bf16 checkpoint. NVFP4 stores some weights in 4 bits, and this way, it shrinks the 501B parameters in BF16 from 1 TB to ~280 GB. Blackwell GPUs run NVFP4 natively but GPUs older than Blackwell like the H200 can't. The FP8 checkpoints are suitable for GPUs older than Blackwell.

A B200 has 180 GB of HBM3e, so two of them (360 GB) can hold the Beam weights, with little room left for activations and the KV cache. Strategy for four B200s (720 GB), which leaves plenty of room for long contexts and concurrent requests. You can also serve it on a full 8xB200 node, or on two B300s at 288 GB each, or even 8xRTX Pro 6000. If you don't have Blackwell hardware, use Inference Providers (serverless) to test Reflection.

Beam comes with day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM.

Install the latest version of transformers.

The easiest way to run Beam is the text-generation pipeline:.

The pipeline returns the whole chat. The last message is Beam's reply, already parsed by the response template.

Going one level lower, use AutoModelForCausalLM and AutoTokenizer.

Beam's tokenizer carries a response template. parse_response reads it and turns the raw output into a message dict, with the reasoning, the answer, and any tool calls in separate fields. This avoids the usual regex for splitting reasoning from answers from tool calls. And the rules ship with the tokenizer, so the parsed structure matches what Beam was trained to produce. The chat template can pre-write part of the assistant turn, which the parser needs to see.

Pass tools to parse_response as well. Beam writes tool-call arguments inline, in its own XML-style grammar, so a bare 7 could be a number or a string. With the tool schemas, the parser casts each argument to its declared type.

It has been revealed that beam's config defines an expert-parallel strategy. Expert parallelism puts each expert on one device. Attention, the dense layers, the embeddings and the LM head are replicated on every device. That is 8B parameters, or 16 GB in BF16. Load the model with a DistributedConfig:.

Recent findings suggest that launch the script with torchrun across 16 H200 GPUs. Each one then holds 78 GB of weights. With 8 GPUs each would hold 139 GB, which leaves no room on a 141 GB H200. The number of devices must divide the number of experts, 256.

Beam has day-0 support in vLLM. The command below serves the BF16 checkpoint with tensor parallelism across 16 GPUs (two 8x H200 nodes) and exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:.

For faster generation, add DFlash2 speculative decoding. A small drafter model proposes up to 15 tokens ahead, and Beam checks them all in one forward pass, so each step can accept several tokens. The cost is a little extra memory for the drafter:.

Both commands start an OpenAI-compatible server, so you can point any OpenAI client at http://localhost:8000/v1. For additional serving configurations, see the proposed Beam recipe for vLLM.

Beam also has day-0 support in SGLang. We recommend serving it with DFlash2 speculative decoding, which both commands below turn on. On Blackwell, the NVFP4 checkpoint fits on 4 B300s:.

On Hopper GPUs, use the FP8 checkpoint on 8 H200s instead. Only three flags change: the checkpoint, the tensor-parallel size (8 instead of 4), and the attention backend (fa3 instead of trtllm_mha, which needs Blackwell):.

Beam is available on Hugging Face Inference Providers, powered by Baseten, Fireworks, and Together, with more to follow soon.

Sources indicate that we are sharing some vibe evals of Reflection Beam-501B-A23B on five tasks, once each at low and high reasoning effort through the Reflection platform. These are vibe evals, not benchmarks. If you’re planning on using Beam, this is a great way to kick the tires and see how it behaves on specific use cases, and importantly, where it wins and loses.

According to recent reports, below is an overview of the prompts we ran and the output traces from the hub. The complete inputs, outputs, API usage, task fixtures, graders and conversation traces are in this public Hugging Face bucket.

* Low's long-context response got all code behavior and all six source citations correct. However, the response did not correspond to the parsers format, so this is partly prompt ambiguity.

Sources indicate that † Low returned the correct answer, but omitted the requested justification. High supplied a correct roots-of-unity proof, independently reviewed.

Industry observers note that don’t take our word for it. Dig into the bucket, rewrite for your use case or project and push Beam to the limit.

It has been revealed that you can fine tune Beam for your own use cases. Here, we share some examples in TRL and Miles to get you started on supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.

The quickest way to adapt Beam to your own data is supervised fine-tuning with TRL's SFTTrainer. To keep memory manageable, we train LoRA adapters with PEFT rather than updating all 501B parameters: We used TRL’s SFTTrainer to adapt Beam to a simple goal: keep its reasoning in the language requested by the user. We fine-tuned on Multilingual-Thinking with LoRA, which trains a small set of adapter weights while keeping the base model frozen.

The setup combines model sharding at load time, expert parallelism, FlashAttention 4 and sequence packing. LoRA SFT fits on a single node with 8 B300 GPUs, reaching around 19,000 tokens per second. The corresponding H100 setup uses four nodes.

After one epoch of Multilingual-Thinking, Beam reasoned in the requested language on 16 out of 16 held-out prompts, compared with 3 out of 16 for the base model. This small evaluation measures language adherence, rather than the correctness of the reasoning itself.

Training loss (left) and mean token accuracy (right) during a separate 500-step run on a reasoning subset of open-r1/Mixture-of-Thought, using one 8-GPU B300 node. These training metrics are from the official TRL example PR.

Reflection and RadixArk built a recipe that trains the model with GRPO in Miles, in BF16. You can update the full model or use LoRA to train adapters while keeping the base weights frozen. Megatron trains, SGLang generates the rollouts, and Miles publishes the new weights to the rollout engines after each update. We reviewed the recipe.

The recipe runs GRPO on DAPO-Math-17K and evaluates on AIME25. Build the image, download the data, and submit the job to a Ray cluster of twelve 8x H200 nodes:.

Sample: 32 prompts are passed to the model with 8 responses each. Two SGLang engines serve the rollouts on 16 GPUs each.

Score: the boxed answer is checked against the label, with a soft penalty for responses near the length limit.

Update: one optimizer step on all 256 samples. Group-relative advantages with truncated importance sampling, no KL or entropy penalty.

Train in parallel: tensor parallelism 8, expert parallelism 8, data parallelism 8, with sequence parallelism and full recompute.

In a recent development, optimizer: Adam at a constant 1e-6. Gradients in BF16, master weights in FP32, moments in BF16. The optimizer state streams through node-local NVMe, so each trainer node needs 2 TB of scratch.

It has been revealed that evaluate: AIME25 every five rollouts, eight samples per problem. A checkpoint is saved every twenty.

The next rollout is generated while the current one trains, so responses are one upgrade behind. Add --resume to continue from the last checkpoint. execute-colocate runs the same recipe on eight nodes, with every GPU training and serving in turn.

You can also run GRPO with LoRA on four 8× H200 nodes: 16 GPUs for training and 16 for rollouts. The recipe trains rank-16 adapters on Beam’s attention, dense MLP, and expert layers while keeping the base weights frozen. Only adapter weights are synchronized with SGLang, and the optimizer state stays in GPU memory, removing the need for NVMe optimizer offloading.

If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build a space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. To inspire you, here are a few things we built.

You can check out the agent trace of how Beam built this in pi in this trace. If you want to try the demo out, download the source code or read the setup instructions.

According to recent reports, we wanted to see whether Beam could make faster progress by splitting a programming task across agents. We paired Beam with the open-source Pi coding agent and compared three setups: 1. one agent working alone, 2. five persistent peers collaborating through a shared Git repository, and 3. a lead agent delegating work to asynchronous subagents. The harness ran on Hugging Face jobs with inference through Reflection’s platform API.

Industry observers note that for the tasks, we used ProgramBench: agents must recreate a program from its compiled executable and documentation, without seeing its source code or the evaluator’s tests. Each setup had the same 8M API-token ceiling and two-hour solver limit per task, shared across its agents. We saved implementation snapshots and evaluated them against fixed hidden-test suites from the ProgramBench-Tests dataset.

Sources indicate that our score-versus-latency plot shows the average fraction of tests passed. The time axis uses fixed reference rates for model tokens plus measured tool time, rather than elapsed wall time. We initially ran five tasks. The current figure shows a post-hoc subset of jq, xsv, FIGlet, and hexyl; ripgrep was excluded across all three setups because grading its saved artifacts was too slow. The published results retain all 15 original episodes.

You can inspect the runs in the Trackio dashboard, explore the published result data, and reuse the study harness.

Decision models are all the rage at the moment because they’re super fast and practical for many use cases. We started with Beam in Pi after Beam’s quota ran out to train and evaluate a custom decision model for developer incident triage.

We wanted to see whether a coding agent could turn an incident-triage policy into a small, fast decision model. The task was to read a developer incident and choose the responsible team, its severity, and whether someone should be pinged immediately. Using Unsloth, we fine-tuned Qwen3.5-0.8B to score these choices directly.

First, the workflow built a synthetic dataset containing 2.3k incidents split by incident cluster for training, calibration, and testing. We trained a LoRA adapter and decision head for three epochs, with a 4-bit backbone, on one H100 80GB on the Science Slurm cluster.

In a recent development, for a baseline, we prompted the unadapted model with the full triage policy and ticket, without examples, and asked it to generate the three decisions as JSON. On the same 320 synthetic test tickets, the fine-tuned decision model got all three answers correct on 76.25%, versus 4.69% for prompted zero-shot. Mean ticket latency fell from 1,218.06 ms to 102.58 ms, an 11.9× speedup.

SIMMTECH’s board approved two KRW 150 billion private perpetual bond issues on November 26, 2026 to expand production of AI-oriented SOCAMM module substrates and high-layer MSAP substrates, according to convertible-bond and bond-with-warrants decisions filed through South Korea’s DART corporate-disclosure system.

Sources indicate that the Series 11 securities are unsecured private perpetual convertible bonds; Series 12 comprises unsecured, non-detachable private perpetual bonds with warrants. Each filing designates the full amount as facility funds for the two substrate categories from December 2026 through December 2027, with no allocation to working capital or debt repayment. Subscriptions occurred on the approval date, while cash payment is scheduled for December 4, 2026, so the disclosures cover an approved financing before the proceeds are received.

SIMMTECH approved KRW 274.2 billion in an August 25, 2026 capacity-investment decision for a dedicated AI-oriented SOCAMM module-substrate factory and additional high-layer MSAP substrate capacity through December 31, 2027. That decision cited increasing demand for both product categories and identified internal resources or external financing, excluding a rights offering, as the funding sources. The November approvals supply a defined external financing structure for the same two substrate categories, rather than marking a change in product direction.

Recent findings suggest that both series carry an initial 3% coupon and maturity yield and mature on December 4, 2056. Full conversion or warrant exercise for either series would produce 1,409,906 common shares at KRW 106,390 per share, equivalent to 3.54% of SIMMTECH’s existing shares for that series. Conversion and exercise rights open on December 4, 2027 and run through November 4, 2056.

Sources indicate that the Series 11 capital-securities terms and corresponding Series 12 terms allow SIMMTECH to defer interest at its discretion, with unpaid amounts accumulating additional interest. The manufacturer can also extend maturity on the same issuance conditions, while holders have no right to demand early redemption.

From December 4, 2029, the coupon and maturity yield increase by four percentage points, followed by annual one-percentage-point increases capped at 19%. SIMMTECH may redeem either series quarterly beginning on that date, giving it a scheduled route to retire the securities as their cost rises.

Industry observers note that SIMMTECH reported preliminary third-quarter 2026 results showing consolidated revenue of KRW 535.9 billion, up 43.7% from a year earlier, and operating profit of KRW 101.8 billion, up 721.6%. The figures are unaudited and subject to change during accounting review. The resulting operating margin is roughly 19%, calculated from the reported revenue and operating profit.

The disclosures frame the expansion’s financing trade-off: SIMMTECH has arranged long-dated capital for AI-substrate capacity, investors hold routes into common shares, and the organization faces escalating coupons on securities left outstanding. The balance among conversion, warrant exercise and redemption after the step-ups begin will shape whether the larger effect comes through dilution or interest expense.

Industry observers note that A product team can ship the same model to two customers and inherit two different compliance problems. One customer uses it to draft internal notes; another uses it in a consequential decision. The technology may look similar while the legal role, evidence requirements and affected people change.

Industry observers note that that is what makes AI regulation an operating challenge in 2027. Businesses will need a usable account of where the product may go, what it may do there and which obligations travel with the use case.

The timetable itself requires care. The European Commission indicates the AI Omnibus entered into force in July 2026. Its current AI Act FAQ distinguishes high-risk application dates, including December 2, 2027 for Annex III systems and August 2, 2028 for certain product-related systems. Older summaries can therefore mislead planning. These forecasts use the position available on November 3, 2026; subsequent legal changes could alter the calendar.

The promise of one global product will increasingly require a more detailed release package. In 2027, suppliers will publish market-specific configurations or documents that distinguish the customer's role and intended use. The underlying model can remain shared. What changes is the precision with which the manufacturer explains the conditions under which the finished service can be offered.

Recent findings suggest that one underlying model can support many products, and one product can create different obligations depending on its purpose, people and deployment location. A general writing assistant and an employment-screening system do not become equivalent simply because they share model infrastructure.

According to recent reports, the Commission's explanation of AI Act scope distinguishes providers, deployers and general-purpose model suppliers, including some actors outside the EU whose products enter its market. That role-based structure makes a single undifferentiated global compliance statement increasingly difficult to use.

Industry observers note that my expectation is practical differentiation: market-specific documentation, transparency settings, intended-use boundaries and enterprise support. This need not require separate models for every country. Over-separating the technical stack can itself create maintenance and testing problems. The more likely architecture is a shared product with explicit regional conditions and a controlled process for deciding which configurations may be sold where.

It has been revealed that look for documentation that identifies the jurisdiction, product role and applicable use case. Regional server hosting by itself would not establish this forecast. A meaningful compliance package should explain which obligations it supports and what the customer still needs to do.

Industry observers note that map market access requirements onto the release process before promising worldwide availability. Buyers should ask whether the supplier's documentation covers their actual use case. A generic claim that a model is compliant can obscure obligations that arise only when the buyer deploys it.

Industry observers note that A procurement team cannot wait until a deadline to discover that the purchased system lacks the oversight or records its deployment requires. In 2027, buyers of EU high-risk applications will ask earlier for operational evidence. That will move compliance discussion into demonstrations, acceptance criteria and contracts, where the customer can still influence what is delivered.

A legal deadline does not coincide neatly with an enterprise buying cycle. Contracts, integration work and staff training can begin months before deployment. Buyers therefore have a reason to ask for the evidence needed to operate the system while they still have negotiating leverage.

In a recent development, the Commission's enforcement overview distinguishes the responsibilities of authorities and the timing of obligations. The Council's AI Act timeline also records the evolving implementation sequence. These official materials describe the legal framework; they do not prove that every supplier is ready.

According to recent reports, who receives an alert? What can a supervisor override? Which logs can the customer inspect? The weakness will be performative documentation that describes capabilities the actual product configuration does not provide.

Industry observers note that look for assurance documents tied to a named version and deployment context. Public tenders and completed supplier packages will be stronger evidence than statements of intention. Repeated postponements of implementation dates would reduce the immediate pressure behind this prediction.

Prepare a reusable evidence package, then adapt it to the customer's role and deployment. Buyers should connect contractual promises with acceptance tests. Oversight and logging obligations need operational owners and budgets, rather than being left entirely to legal review at signature.

Industry observers note that A sandbox is most valuable when it resolves a specific uncertainty. Participation can become misleading if it is presented as unrestricted approval. In 2027, public sandbox outputs will make testing boundaries and practical lessons more visible. The useful result may be a narrower product scope or a clearer obligation—an outcome less promotional than endorsement, but far more actionable.

Sources indicate that testing under supervision can help a developer understand how an emerging product fits a legal framework. It does not automatically establish that every later configuration, customer or use case is acceptable. The value of a sandbox lies partly in making those boundaries explicit.

In a recent development, the Council's implementation timeline identifies the revised timetable for national sandboxes. The Commission FAQ explains their role in supporting innovation. My forecast is about published practical outputs during the year, not an assumption that every member state will produce comparable results on the same schedule.

Recent findings suggest that publication may be limited by confidentiality and the resources of participating authorities. That is why the forecast does not require a comprehensive public register of every experiment. Still, examples of specific lessons would help smaller suppliers more than promotional announcements saying that a company has joined a program.

Look for identified use cases, test conditions and the distinction between advice, experimentation and authorization. A participant describing sandbox admission as a general government endorsement would be weak evidence of mature implementation. Guidance that changes a product's scope would be much more informative.

Sources indicate that use a sandbox to resolve specific uncertainties and preserve the resulting conditions. Proposal for obligations outside the test environment. It has been revealed that A legal change matters to a customer when somebody explains what it changes in the product. In 2027, more suppliers will connect regulatory updates to configurations, documentation or intended-use limits. That will require legal interpretation and product management to share a working process, so customers receive a specific action rather than another broad announcement about the importance of compliance.

Recent findings suggest that compliance cannot remain a one-time launch assessment when both the legal framework and the product are changing. A new downstream use, a revised model or a changed implementation date can invalidate assumptions used in an earlier sales process.

Sources indicate that the difference between the 2026 Omnibus change and earlier implementation summaries illustrates the operational problem. Separately, the Commission's One Europe, One Market roadmap includes further policy initiatives; proposed legislation must be distinguished from enacted obligations. A roadmap target should never be presented as a current legal duty.

The practical capability will be a controlled link between legal interpretation and product behavior. Suppliers will need to explain what changed, which customers are affected and whether action is required. Too many undifferentiated notices can create alert fatigue, while silent changes can leave customers operating under obsolete assumptions.

Look for dated notices with an identified legal trigger and a specific customer action or configuration change. A generic regulatory newsletter would not qualify. Clear separation of proposals, adopted rules and effective obligations will be a useful sign of quality.

Give product, legal and customer-success teams a shared change process. Customers need notification rights that fit their deployment cycle. Maintain a dated record of the assumptions behind market access decisions so that a change can be assessed without reconstructing the entire product history.

It has been revealed that the businesses best placed to navigate AI regulation will be able to explain their products with unusual precision. Which role, which use, which market and which date are operational questions. Answering them well can make expansion more predictable even while the surrounding rules continue to evolve.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • TorchNeuron provides a newly introduced native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium.
  • TorchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a new backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP.
  • 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TorchNeuron provides a newly introduced native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels natively support it, making it easier than ever to run models on Trainium and to share them on the HF hub.

TorchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a new backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP. Read the Pytorch blog to learn more about TorchNeuron.

Starting Oct. 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta. Researchers and developers will be able to install it with pip install torch-neuronx.

To date, the Hugging Face experience on AWS Trainium and Inferentia — AI chips designed respectively for cost-effective training and inference at scale — has been delivered through optimum-neuron. This library relies on the torch-neuronx package, which is based on PyTorch XLA. It was the natural choice at the time, but it meant thinking like a compiler: lazy tensors instead of eager execution, static shapes only, a recompilation for every graph break. Optimum Neuron existed to hide that complexity, and maintained custom code (modeling classes, trainers, etc) to do so.

It has been revealed that torchNeuron changes this. It integrates directly into PyTorch and exposes neuron as a native device, with eager execution, PyTorch's own distributed primitives (DTensor, FSDP2) and torch.compile.

Sources indicate that for the Hugging Face libraries, Trainium becomes a device like any other: Transformers, Diffusers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL run on it directly, with the same classes and scripts you would use on any other accelerator. From now on, we recommend that Neuron owners use these libraries directly instead of going through Optimum Neuron.

In a recent development, text generation is now natively supported in Transformers for a wide range of models. With TorchNeuron, 89% of the top 100 most-used text-generation model architectures are supported out of the box, compared to 46% with Optimum Neuron v0.4.5. You just need to pass the device_map=neuron argument in your code and your model will be moved to the Neuron devices.

Recent findings suggest that the following is an example of text-generation with tensor parallelism, which will enable to fully benefit from your Neuron instance. Note that it uses a static cache for generation as this is strongly recommended with Neuron to prevent frequent recompilations.

Recent findings suggest that now that Neuron is a native PyTorch device, training on Trainium uses the same Hugging Face libraries as any other accelerator: Transformers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL. You no longer need a dedicated trainer or a Neuron-specific fork of the model code. A standard TRL fine-tuning script runs on a Trainium instance with only a few Neuron-specific settings.

Here is a supervised fine-tuning script built on TRL's SFTTrainer. If you have fine-tuned a model with TRL on GPUs before, it should look familiar.

Parallelism is handled natively by Transformers. You put a DistributedConfig with the tensor-parallel (TP) and FSDP sizes in model_init_kwargs, SFTTrainer passes it to from_pretrained, and the model is sharded as its weights are loaded. The Trainer sees that the model is already distributed and does not wrap it again. You don't need an --fsdp flag or an Accelerate FSDP config.

It has been revealed that nothing in the script is tied to Trainium: the same code runs on any hardware. A few things are worth knowing when you run it on Trainium:.

It has been revealed that the command below releases training with torchrun, which starts one process per NeuronCore. TP_SIZE and FSDP_SIZE set the parallelism layout, and their product is the number of processes: here 4 x 8 = 32, matching --nproc_per_node. The 32 processes form a 4 x 8 grid. Tensor parallelism splits each layer across the 4 cores of a TP group, and FSDP shards the parameters, gradients and optimizer state across the 8 TP groups.

We ran it on 8 Trainium2 chips (32 NeuronCores), which is half a trn2.48xlarge instance.

Industry observers note that training runs to completion, and trainer.save_model writes a standard Transformers checkpoint. Nothing in it is tied to Neuron: you can push it to the Hugging Face Hub as is and load it on any other hardware.

Many pipelines from the Diffusers library are compatible with TorchNeuron in eager and compiled mode. FLUX.1-dev, FLUX.2, Qwen-Image, Qwen-Image-2.1 and H3 are also compatible with tensor parallelism to make the most of your Neuron devices. The following is an example showing how you can use TP:.

You can run this piece of code with: NEURON_LOGICAL_NC_CONFIG=2 torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 run.py.

Recent findings suggest that more and more pipleines will be compatible with TP. If a pipeline you like is not, you can also add support for it following this guide.

Recent findings suggest that make sure to check out the kernels from the Neuron team as more and more Neuron kernels will become available on the Hub to speed up your models. Neuron kernels can be written using the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI), which gives lower control to optimize operations. This way, users can run their own custom operations and share them on the hub.

You can use for example this kernel to speed up your vision transformers with up to a x2.4 speedup on Trainium!

Special thanks to the AWS team for their work on TorchNeuron and for their reactivity to our feedback to make the HF integration as good as possible.

Improving Human Impersonation, as the Web Closes Up Against AI

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Web scraping used to be a more casual affair: Robotic Process Automation (RPA) routines created on a write-once, run-many basis – humans recording their browsing actions, refining them through various automation processes, and setting them to run at intervals, unattended, in order to obtain data from websites that only want real humans (or paying clients) accessing them and their data – and which take measures to repel automated browsing of this kind.
  • In a recent development, of course, domains subject to this treatment often considered RPA to be more akin to ‘data exfiltration’ and/or ‘hacking’ than any definition of ‘browsing’.
  • Since publicly-available data has become a truly valuable resource for AI companies (rather than the insipid ‘Data is the latest gold’ rhetoric of ten years ago), at least 60% of reputable sites have been found to be repelling an AI crawler – a rise (in 2025) from 23%, two years earlier.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Web scraping used to be a more casual affair: Robotic Process Automation (RPA) routines created on a write-once, run-many basis – humans recording their browsing actions, refining them through various automation processes, and setting them to run at intervals, unattended, in order to obtain data from websites that only want real humans (or paying clients) accessing them and their data – and which take measures to repel automated browsing of this kind.

In a recent development, of course, domains subject to this treatment often considered RPA to be more akin to ‘data exfiltration’ and/or ‘hacking’ than any definition of ‘browsing’. Prior to the current era of AI, web scraping emerged from obscurity quite rarely, as a marginal form of pest; until LinkedIn introduced an ultimately-doomed lawsuit against HiQ Labs, an ‘intelligent automation’ provider, and one of many corporate concerns that challenged LinkedIn’s right to harvest publicly, profit privately.

Since publicly-available data has become a truly valuable resource for AI companies (rather than the insipid ‘Data is the latest gold’ rhetoric of ten years ago), at least 60% of reputable sites have been found to be repelling an AI crawler – a rise (in 2025) from 23%, two years earlier.

In practical terms, defending against any kind of web scraper is about pattern-matching, and looking for evidence of algorithmic access, such as screenshotting non-selectable text, or polling the CSS stylesheets, or the other underlying structures of a page.

These actions in themselves, no matter who or what executes them, are often considered evidence of automated processes rather than human interaction; personally – and especially at Yandex – I often have to complete CAPTCHAs because I make ‘uncommon’ or technical queries; and the more protective and protected domains are generally intolerant of anything but ‘mom ‘n pop’ baseline browsing behavior.

However, that’s still a relatively rare and heavy-handed experience. For the most part, anti-scraper logic and algorithms are looking not so much at the actions as for the way they are enacted – and especially for repetitive usage patterns for keyboard and mouse interaction. This could mean that a played-back RPA human interaction that works at first will shortly become blacklisted, because its lack of variation reveals it over time as a routine, and not a person.

Because of the growth of AI scraping, the tools of the RPA industry have suddenly become of great interest both to AI and intelligence companies that consider publicly available data ‘fair game’ in spite of any interstitial defenses (a stance theoretically supported by LinkedIn’s defeat in the aforementioned lawsuit – at least in the US); and the defending domains that in most (but not all) cases don’t have quite enough market capture to retain their profitable user base behind a login-wall, and would prefer to keep access open.

In the latter case, the companies have hardened themselves against the customary dedicated ‘headless’ browsers common in RPA, and against dedicated RPA frameworks such as Microsoft’s Playwright, and its derivatives and forks.

The security sector has taken an interest lately in whether AI-powered web agents can actually still be recognized by sites that are on the defensive against such activities. After all, these incursions may not be running on a CRON job, but neither are they ‘human’.

In this regard, a latest paper† from Canada proposes an AI-powered web agent designed to test the effectiveness of current anti-bot defenses. By combining a modified version of Chromium with AI models trained to reproduce human mouse and keyboard activity, the new system achieved access (non-rejection of browsing) in 89% of tests on a benchmark of protected websites – 12 percentage points above the best previously-published result:.

Comparative test results for bypassing eleven categories of web bot protection. Figures indicate successful page access as percentages, with test counts in parentheses. The new paper’s system, DarkAgent, achieved the highest overall score across 80 tests, compared with previously published results for nine other browser configurations. Source.

The system, dubbed DarkAgent, consists of Browsium, a customized Chromium browser engineered to conceal evidence of automated control; and Behavium, a framework incorporating two machine learning models: MouseGen, and KeyboardGen, which, together, simulate human interaction with the browser:.

Industry observers note that the DarkAgent workflow. Browsing decisions are translated into simulated human interactions, executed through Browsium’s native input mechanisms. The resulting page changes are fed back to the planning agent to determine its next action.

The architecture, shown above, addresses four categories of evidence available to bot detection systems, namely interaction patterns; browser and device characteristics; evidence of automated browser control; and network protocol characteristics.

The aforementioned KeyboardGen was trained on the Aalto keyboard dataset, derived from a study of 136 million keystrokes, to reproduce typing rhythms, errors and corrections. MouseGen was trained on the Boğaziçi Mouse Dynamics dataset, with additional scrolling data sourced from the Attentive Cursor dataset:.

Examples of mouse movements, in coordinate and interpreted form, from the Attentive Cursor Dataset. Source.

Both generators use Transformer architectures, while the browser modifications were implemented through conventional programming. OpenAI’s GPT-4.1 was used to decide which actions to perform during the benchmark tests.

According to recent reports, the browser’s reported identity and the simulated user behavior are coordinated throughout each session, so that the various signals presented to a website remain consistent with one another. To support this, a separate JavaScript-based environment within Chromium allows the agent to inspect web pages without exposing its presence to the website’s own scripts:.

Comparison of conventional browser automation (top), using the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) to inspect and control web pages, and the newly introduced paper’s approach (bottom), where a private communication channel reduces the evidence of automated activity visible to websites.

Recent findings suggest that the simulated mouse movements and keystrokes are then processed by the browser as genuine user input, with the same trusted status granted to physical mouse and keyboard activity. Variations in mouse trajectories and typing patterns, learned from recorded human activity, facilitate different sequences of movements and actin timings, reflecting the natural inconsistencies of human interaction.

DarkAgent was evaluated using Stealth Bench V1, a benchmark developed by Browser Use, comprising 80 short mouse and keyboard tasks on live websites, requiring no login and covering eleven categories of protection: Cloudflare; PerimeterX; DataDome; Akamai; reCAPTCHA; Kasada; Shape; GeeTest; hCaptcha; Temu; and (unspecified) site-specific anti-bot systems.

The tests were conducted in August 2026*, using geographically-matched residential proxies, with success measured solely by whether page access was obtained, and discounting task completion. Comparative results were drawn from earlier baseline tests conducted by the benchmark’s authors.

To establish the individual contributions of DarkAgent’s components, 30 browsing sessions were scheduled for each of 18 configurations on a website hosted by the researchers, with identical prompts, tasks, planning models, and limits on the number of actions.

For this, standard Chromium and Browsium were tested with and without Behavium, and with MouseGen and KeyboardGen enabled independently.

Additional comparisons were made with Firefox; Camoufox; the Playwright derivative Patchright; CloakBrowser; and publicly-available human behavior simulators Ghost Cursor; HumanTyping; and CloakBrowser’s Humanize.

The browsing sessions were evaluated using FP-Agent (an existing bot-detection system); additionally, JA4DB (a database of network connection fingerprints) was used to check whether the browser’s reported identity was consistent with its network activity.

Beyond the initial Stealth Bench V1 results presented earlier, all browsing sessions conducted without behavioral simulation were identified as automated by FP-Agent, while every session conducted with Behavium enabled in either Chromium or Browsium was classified as human:.

Bot detection results across 18 browser configurations, based on 30 sessions per configuration. P(Human) indicates the average probability of human activity assigned by FP-Agent, Verdict indicates the most frequent classification, and the final column identifies the browser engine inferred from the network connection.

Similar results were obtained with Ghost Cursor and CloakBrowser’s Humanize, indicative of a weakness in FP-Agent (which doesn’t examine how fast the mouse moves, or how its speed changes).

In a recent development, in AgentShield tests, all 139 form-filling sessions from the benchmark’s existing automated agents were flagged as bot activity, as were all ten sessions conducted with Browsium using standard automated input. With DarkAgent and CloakBrowser + Humanize, all ten trials per configuration were completed successfully without detection:.

It has been revealed that results of the AgentShield form-completion tests, showing successful submissions, bot detection rates, detection scores, mouse movements and keypress durations. DarkAgent and CloakBrowser + Humanize escaped detection, though DarkAgent’s keypress durations were considerably closer to those of human people.

In a recent development, when newly introduced fields appeared in the form, they were attended to by DarkAgent within an average of 3.74 seconds, compared to 4.72 seconds for human owners. The greater variation in human response times suggests, the authors contend, that bots could still be identified by the length and consistency of the pauses between actions.

Although this almost-impenetrable paper is not likely to gather many adherents to the cause, web scraping is one of the most interesting challenges for the dataset-builder and proponent of agentic AI.

However, it’s fast-becoming a Quixotic pursuit; even sites that may be indifferent to data acquisition routines are now likely to become defended against RPA and agentic AI in the very near future, simply because it is becoming a default position.

While data of the kind dealt with in this research can be extracted from human engagement farms in Asia, such data will inevitably form recognizable patterns in the aggregate, so that the routines that are part of them can be specifically blocked – a familiar pattern in a newly introduced cold war that’s starting to heat up.

Projecting the scenario to an extreme, truly effective RPA countermeasures could signal the wholesale revival of the crowdsourced worker – lately an eclipsed figure.

According to recent reports, † Titled ‘Are Web Agents Still Detectable? Stress-Testing Bot Defenses with Coordinated Evasion’.

* Relevant only because GPT4.1 was available then.

#162327. MPS in PyTorch 2.15

MPS in PyTorch 2.15

📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1371 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15!
  • A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face.
  • If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15! FP8 arrives on MPS, language-model decoding gets faster paths through linear layers and softmax and latest Metal kernels tackle some surprisingly expensive parts of audio, video and training workloads.

A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face. We contribute across PyTorch, and one of our focus areas is the MPS backend, where the goal is to make your Mac a first-class place to run and train PyTorch models. At the start of 2026, running even small models on MPS often meant working around unsupported operations, performance cliffs and unexpected memory growth. So we run real models from the Hugging Face Hub across language, image and video, find where MPS falls short and fix it upstream in PyTorch, more and more often by replacing MPSGraph with dedicated Metal kernels. Much of this post is the result of that work, done together with the PyTorch maintainers and community contributors.

If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:.

Industry observers note that you'll need an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 15 or later and Python 3.11 or later (see the 2.15 compatibility matrix). If your OS is too old or no Metal GPU is available, the MPS availability check now tells you why.

To try the release candidate in a separate environment:.

FP8 gives you another way to save memory on your Mac. PyTorch 2.15 adds torch.float8_e4m3fn tensors on MPS: one byte per value, half the storage of FP16 or BF16.

You can multiply these tensors with F.scaled_mm, which supports both tensorwise and rowwise scaling. Here's a small example with one scale per tensor:.

Recent findings suggest that every LLM has a prefill phase and a decode phase. During decode, each upcoming token goes through the model as a single row, so the major matrix multiplications turn into matrix-vector products. PyTorch 2.15 speeds up both kinds of layers that dominate this step: dense linear layers and mixture-of-experts layers.

Sources indicate that MPS has had GEMV kernels for torch.mm since 2.14, but F.linear still went through MPSGraph. PyTorch 2.15 connects them to F.linear, so the common [1, 1, hidden_size] decoding input uses them directly, with eligible bias additions fused in. Across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models, that's a 1.23× geometric-mean speedup. The biggest wins land on small projections, such as the gates in MoE models, where the old path left most of the memory bandwidth unused. Large layers and LM heads were already close to bandwidth-bound, so they stay near 1×.

Recent findings suggest that A mixture-of-experts layer sends different numbers of tokens to each expert. Grouped matmul handles those uneven groups in a single operation, and 2.15 gives MPS a native implementation.

Sources indicate that in 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. The newly introduced Metal kernels read the offsets directly on the GPU, using Metal Performance Primitives where available and a separate Metal path elsewhere. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get their own kernel as well.

For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16:.

Industry observers note that the decoding kernel highlights up directly in token throughput. On an M3 Ultra with torch.compile, MoE models generate about 1.3× more tokens per second:.

Working with complex tensors gets easier. complex64 LU factorization, LU solve and triangular solve now run on MPS, which also unlocks the operations and gradients built on them, such as complex determinants. Here's a small system solved directly on the GPU:.

Recent findings suggest that small matrices get fast kernels too. For camera geometry and image transformations, batches of FP32 matrices up to 4 × 4 are inverted in a single Metal kernel that combines factorization and solving. Larger problems get attention as well: QR uses blocked updates, and triangular solves turn much of their work into efficient matrix multiplication.

Gated DeltaNet workloads get a dedicated fast path for batches of 16 × 16, 32 × 32 and 64 × 64 FP32 triangular systems with at least eight right-hand sides.

It has been revealed that SVD is also more robust at numerical extremes. It now correctly handles very small singular values, very large or very small input magnitudes and basis completion with full_matrices=True, which in turn makes pseudoinverse and least-squares results more reliable.

Recent findings suggest that audio models, video decoders and training loops have their own expensive operations. This release gives several of them upcoming paths through Metal:.

It has been revealed that token sampling gets faster in 2.15 as well. softmax and log_softmax now run on dedicated Metal kernels, and large vocabularies benefit the most: an FP32 softmax over a [1, 128256] row of logits drops from 57 µs to 7 µs, about 8× faster than the MPSGraph version. The speedup holds across other common vocabulary sizes:.

Industry observers note that one of the most striking results in this release comes from the constant-padding change. The VAE decode in Wan-AI/Wan2.2-TI2V-5B-Diffusers makes 8,764 padding calls over a full 28-tile decode. With padding on Metal, peak driver memory drops from about 270 GiB to 8 GiB:.

You can now pick which MPS stream runs your work, directly from Python. torch.mps.Stream and the torch.mps.stream context manager provide the interface, and Tensor.record_stream lets the allocator track a tensor's use on another stream.

Here's a small example that sends work to a separate stream and synchronizes before reading the result:.

Recent findings suggest that several more operations now run on MPS: torch.frexp, torch.logspace, torch.take and Tensor.put_, torch.heaviside, torch.special.laguerre_polynomial_l and unsigned-integer comparisons. logspace doesn't yet support integer or boolean outputs with more than one element.

Attention gets a correctness fix too: the MPS math implementation of scaled dot-product attention now handles batch and head broadcasting correctly.

Work on 2.16 is already well underway. Some of the changes below have landed on main and are available in the nightlies; others are still in review, so details may change before the release.

According to recent reports, once a model's decode path no longer contains any MPSGraph ops, the GPU only starts on a token after the CPU has finished encoding all of its kernels. PyTorch 2.16 commits the command buffer every 16 kernels, so the GPU gets to work while the CPU is still encoding the rest. For compiled BF16 decoding at a 2048-token context:.

Sources indicate that scaled dot-product attention is dropping MPSGraph completely: every shape will run on Metal kernels, with dedicated vector kernels for decoding and Metal Performance Primitives for half-precision prefill on newer macOS versions. The shapes that used to fall back to MPSGraph benefit the most. On an M5 Pro, decoding with grouped-query attention (32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 80, 4K context) drops from 465 µs to 65 µs, and a 4K × 4K prefill with head dim 40 goes from 42 ms to 6 ms.

The move away from MPSGraph continues. Batch norm forward and backward are in progress, while MSE loss (up to 12× faster on small inputs), std_mean and var_mean (up to 4× faster) and bincount have already landed. bincount is the most dramatic: when most values fall into a single bin, counting 4 million integers used to take 6.8 seconds and now takes half a millisecond.

Bundled shaders will build for Metal 3.1 by default, with Metal 4 versions compiled only for the kernels that need them. That shrinks libtorch_cpu.dylib by about 25%, from 384 MiB to 287 MiB, and lays the groundwork for Metal 4.1 shaders with faster matmuls and native FP8 matrix multiplication.

It has been revealed that pyTorch 2.15 brings FP8 to the Mac, faster LLM decoding for dense and MoE models, more linear algebra on the GPU and a long list of operations moved from MPSGraph to dedicated Metal kernels. Give the release candidate a try!
