Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2042 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, language models can do a lot.
  • Say a customer calls your support line.
  • In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, language models can do a lot. They write, summarize, translate, and call tools. But they're only a small part of what machine learning can do.

Say a customer calls your support line. First, you want to know what they stated (speech recognition). Then, you want to decide where to send them (decision). You could hand both to a language model, but there are models built for each that are better, faster, and less expensive.

In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift. With AnyLanguageModel and swift-huggingface now on their 1.x releases, we're extending the same approach to speech and decisions: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of model.

Today we're announcing two packages:.

Both packages can download open models from the Hugging Face Hub and run them on device.

In a recent development, computers have been transcribing speech for decades, and in the past few years, they've gotten very good at it. Apple platforms already have an API for it. macOS 26 and iOS 26 introduced SpeechAnalyzer, Apple's new speech-to-text API. You add modules such as SpeechTranscriber and SpeechDetector to an analyzer, give it a file or a stream of audio buffers, and read results from async sequences as they arrive. AssetInventory installs the models, so your app decides when downloads happen.

Sources indicate that it's a well-designed API, but the only engine behind it is Apple's. AnySpeechRecognizer keeps the API and lets you choose the engine:.

The package mirrors SpeechAnalyzer, SpeechTranscriber, DictationTranscriber, SpeechDetector, and AssetInventory, with Apple's Speech framework as the default engine. If your code uses that shared API, changing the import is enough. To use Parakeet instead, change only how you create the transcriber:.

The steps for installing assets, running the analyzer, and reading results stay the same. The README has a complete example and lists the differences from Apple's framework.

Parakeet v3 is NVIDIA's Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3. It's a polyglot: it recognizes 25 European languages and works out which one it's hearing, so you don't pass a locale.

Parakeet Ultra is Moondream's post-trained take on v3. It was more accurate in most of our measurements.

Parakeet Unified is NVIDIA's English-only Parakeet.

All three Parakeets run on the package's own Core ML runtime, which supports file and live input, volatile results, word timing, and word confidence.

Industry observers note that qwen3-ASR is Alibaba's speech model, in 0.6B and 1.7B sizes. It recognizes 30 languages and 22 Chinese dialects, including Mandarin, Cantonese, Japanese, and Korean, which Parakeet doesn't cover. It detects the language automatically, or you can set one:.

According to recent reports, qwen3-ASR gives one final result for each segment of up to 40 seconds, without volatile results, word timing, or confidence. It runs on the GPU and is slower than Parakeet, so it's better suited to transcribing files than live input.

Sources indicate that to add another engine, implement SpeechRecognitionModel for its configuration and SpeechRecognitionExecutor for one module's session. The README includes a small provider that reports placeholder text to help you get started.

To run these models in apps, we converted them to Core ML and published them on the Hub:.

Each repository records its source checkpoint and a checksum for every file, and the package pins it to a fixed revision. The Parakeet repositories add an 8-second encoder for live input, which cuts live analysis time by about a third at the cost of a somewhat higher word error rate. The repository also has the conversion workflows, most of which follow FluidInference's mobius scripts, and checks each conversion against the original model.

According to recent reports, downloads happen only when your app asks for them: about 600 MB for each Parakeet, plus about 590 MB for the live encoder, 0.9 to 2.4 GB for Qwen3-ASR, and about 250 MB for Sortformer. Files go in the standard Hugging Face cache, so a Mac app outside the sandbox shares them with Python and other Hugging Face tools.

When you transcribe a conversation, you often want to know who stated what. That's speaker diarization, and Apple's Speech framework doesn't have a module for it, so AnySpeechRecognizer adds one. SpeakerDiarizer runs NVIDIA's Streaming Sortformer on Core ML alongside an Apple or Parakeet transcriber, on the same timeline:.

It has been revealed that the diarizer tracks up to four speakers, even when they talk over each other. A SpeakerTimeline collects its results and attributes each timed word to a speaker, so you can print a transcript by speaker turn. Like image support in AnyLanguageModel, this goes beyond what Apple's API offers today.

Industry observers note that the diarizer uses Sortformer v2 by default. You can also choose v2.1, which NVIDIA trained with more meeting data and which was more accurate on meetings in our measurements, too.

We measured the package with its hear command-line tool on an M4 Max Mac Studio with macOS 27.0.1. Here are the word error rates on LibriSpeech files of 3 to 8 minutes:.

Sources indicate that parakeet transcribes an hour of audio in about 20 to 40 seconds from a file, or about 1.5 to 2.5 minutes live, with about 100 MB of memory once Core ML has compiled the model. Qwen3-ASR is much slower and needs a few gigabytes of memory. Meetings are hard for everyone: on AMI recordings, where people talk over each other, every engine we tested had a word error rate above 23%.

These numbers come from one machine and a few datasets, so measure with your own hardware and audio. hear evaluate works on your own files, and the repository's natural-speech-eval.py tool reproduces these measurements. So far, we've tested only on macOS 27, not on an iPhone.

Next, we'd like to add more engines, including Core AI on macOS 27 and iOS 27.

AnyDecisionModel is a different story. There's no Apple framework to map onto, and decision models aren't upcoming, exactly.

It's only a decision model if it comes from the Décision region of France; otherwise, it's sparkling zero-shot classification.

In a recent development, what's fresh is the name, a lot of hype, and a crop of models trained to make decisions. We think that's where things are going, so we wanted a Swift API that's ready for them.

Apps often ask language models to make decisions. Is this message urgent? Which team should handle this ticket? How frustrated is this customer? The usual approach is to prompt a language model and parse the text that it generates. That gives you one answer, but doesn't show the probabilities it assigned to the alternatives.

Here's what a decision looks like in Swift:.

Recent findings suggest that urgent is a Double. team is a Choice containing the selected case, a probability for each option, and a confidence value. anger is a Score containing the expected level, a probability for each level, and a confidence value. Because Department conforms to Choosable, team.value is a Department that you can use in an exhaustive switch.

If you've used Foundation Models or AnyLanguageModel, the model-and-session pattern will look familiar. A DecisionSession holds a single state, which can be text or JSON, and every question is about that state. Questions are independent: an answer never becomes input to a later question. To ask several questions at once, pass them to decide(_:) as a batch.

For each question, the MLX backend builds a prompt with a one-token label for each allowed answer, then reads the probability of each label from one forward pass.

Emoji Magnet is a macOS app with a text field above a pile of 343 emoji. Type a phrase, such as "things you wear", and the emoji that match rise out of the pile. Refine it to "things you wear in winter", and the emoji that no longer match fall back.

The app has no built-in keyword rules; the model decides everything at inference time. When you pause typing, it asks the model one yes-or-no question for each emoji, for example:.

In a recent development, the session's state holds the phrase. The demo above uses the hosted Jev backend, which answers all 343 questions in one request, so the emoji settle in about half a second for each phrase. Without a TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY, the app runs Qwen3 4B on your Mac with the MLX backend. That backend uses prefix caching to evaluate the state once, then answers 16 questions per forward pass. On an M4 Max, a group of 16 takes about 0.45 seconds after the model loads. A full pass over all 343 emoji takes about 10 seconds, and each group's results appear as soon as they arrive.

Emoji Magnet is in the AnyDecisionModel-Examples repository.

Reading next-token probabilities works with general-purpose language models, but those models weren't trained to make decisions. Cloudflare's Clef models are an example of a newer approach: a model with a trained decision head that turns a state and a schema of typed questions into decisions, returning probabilities for all allowed options across the questions in one forward pass. Clef-Flash is the 9B variant.

AnyDecisionModel runs Clef-Flash on a Mac with MLX:.

You use the same sessions and questions, but MLXHeadDecisionModel reads each decision from Clef's trained decision head instead of from next-token probabilities. The 4-bit model is a 6.2 GB download, and its model card recommends a Mac with at least 16 GB of memory. Clef can read images and video, but this backend accepts only text and JSON states.

Raw probabilities from language models are often overconfident. The local backends accept a Calibration, which applies a temperature to every answer and a bias to yes-or-no answers. Use separate datasets to fit the calibration and evaluate the results.

It has been revealed that language models can also favor an option because of its position in a list. On the MLX, Core AI, and llama.cpp next-token backends, turn on rotationDebiasing to ask a choice question once for each rotation of the options and average the probabilities. That costs one prompt evaluation per rotation.

Sources indicate that each local choice and score also includes a confidence value based on the entropy of its probabilities. It measures how concentrated the probabilities are, not whether the answer is right, so check the error rate on your own data before you pick a threshold. The next-token backends' diagnostics report how much probability the model assigned to the allowed answers. A low value means it assigned most of the probability elsewhere.

AnyDecisionModel has six backends:.

Industry observers note that the next-token backends label answers "yes" and "no", A to Z, or 0 to 9, so a choice can have at most 26 options, and a score at most 10 levels. Decision heads have no such limit.

Like AnyLanguageModel, the package uses Swift package traits. Without traits, it has no third-party dependencies. You get the core types and the Jev and Ollama backends, which also build on Linux. Enable the MLX, CoreAI, or Llama trait for the local backends.

It has been revealed that both packages require Swift 6.2 or later and macOS 26 or iOS 26 or later. The Parakeet and Sortformer runtimes and the MLX backend require Apple silicon. AnyDecisionModel's MLX build tasks use Xcode's Swift 6.4 or later and the Metal toolchain; Core AI requires Xcode 27 and an OS 27 runtime.

Add the packages to your Package.swift:.

For now, AnyDecisionModel's CoreAI trait can't be combined with AnySpeechRecognizer, because coreai-kit 0.7.3 requires swift-huggingface below 1.0 and AnySpeechRecognizer requires 1.x.

Each README has more examples and details about requirements and backends. AnySpeechRecognizer also includes a command-line tool, hear, that transcribes local files, labels their speakers, and evaluates the results. Every hear command requires --backend apple, --backend parakeet, or --backend qwen; run hear prepare with the same backend and model options before analysis to install the needed assets.

Try them in your apps and tell us what works and what doesn't. Issues and pull requests are welcome on both repositories.

Thanks to NVIDIA for Parakeet, Sortformer, and NeMo, to Moondream for Parakeet Ultra, to FluidInference, whose FluidAudio and mobius projects documented the conventions that the Parakeet runtime and the Core ML conversions follow, to Cloudflare for Clef, and to everyone who contributed to AnyLanguageModel, whose patterns both packages borrow.

Bloomberg reported on November 26, 2026, that SAP was preparing a plan to eliminate at least 10,000 positions as it reshaped its software business for AI, citing people familiar with the matter, in a report carried by CNBC on November 27, 2026.

SAP told CNBC that AI was rapidly changing its business environment, prompting continuous reviews of how its organization and workforce needed to evolve, and that roles and functions would change during its transformation. Its statement added: “Beyond this, no decisions have been made regarding any further measures. We do not comment on speculation.”.

Reuters independently reported on November 27, 2026, that two people familiar with the matter described preparations for a sizeable workforce reduction, with one saying the works council had not yet been informed. SAP employs around 113,000 people worldwide. At the reported minimum, the reduction would be equivalent to roughly 9% of that workforce, calculated from the two figures.

Recent findings suggest that bloomberg’s account said all departments had been asked to identify potential cuts, with product, engineering and sales receiving particular focus. The reported plan follows a 2024 reorganization that eliminated around 10,000 positions, primarily through voluntary exits and retraining. Hiring for newly introduced roles subsequently kept total headcount broadly flat.

CNBC placed the reported plan against CEO Christian Klein’s push toward an AI-first strategy. SAP completed four acquisitions in 2026: Reltio, Dremio, Prior Labs and TechWolf. It also made strategic investments in AI-focused companies including Parloa, n8n and Conduct. Their stated purposes range from organizing corporate data and building models for business information to analyzing workforce skills.

Reuters also reported that Klein and Chief Financial Officer Dominik Asam had indicated at investor events that a workforce reduction was possible. SAP trimmed its outlook in July 2026 as AI-focused deals weighed on earnings, and an SAP executive mentioned in October 2026 that the organization was swapping some costly models used in its products for lower-cost alternatives. Those moves connect the workforce review to a broader effort to control the cost of SAP’s AI expansion.

CNBC cited comparable moves with different rationales. WiseTech Global’s February 2026 plan covered about 2,000 cuts over two years as it integrated AI, while Atlassian’s March 2026 plan called for about 1,600 cuts partly to fund further AI investment. Cloudflare’s May 2026 plan involved more than 1,100 roles as it moved toward an AI-first operating model.

In a recent development, challenger, Gray & Christmas’s October 2026 report reveals that the broader U.S. trend is more mixed. Employers cited AI in 121,401 announced job cuts through October 2026, approximately 20% of the 617,189 total. AI was cited for 1,265 cuts in October, its lowest monthly total of 2026, while market and economic conditions overtook AI as the leading stated reason for the year.

In a recent development, technology remained the largest industry category in Challenger’s U.S. tracking, with 171,501 revealed cuts through October, up 21% from 141,159 in the same period of 2025 and accounting for 28% of the 2026 total. The contrast matters for SAP: its reported initiative is explicitly tied to AI, while the broader technology total includes reductions made for many other reasons.

Industry observers note that for employees, the decisive questions are whether the reported review becomes a formal initiative, when the works council is informed, and whether SAP again combines voluntary exits and retraining with hiring for new roles. Those factors will shape whether the AI overhaul produces a net workforce reduction or another redistribution of roles while the company absorbs the cost of its AI expansion.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Certain personality traits may help explain why some people betray a partner’s trust.
  • Certain personality traits may help explain why some people betray a partner’s trust.
  • Psychopathy, manipulativeness and narcissism are all associated with cheating.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Certain personality traits may help explain why some people betray a partner’s trust.

Certain personality traits may help explain why some people betray a partner’s trust.

Psychopathy, manipulativeness and narcissism are all associated with cheating.

The strongest average link is with psychopathy, closely followed by Machiavellianism.

Narcissism, which involves an inflated sense of self-importance and a need for admiration, has the weakest link.

Impulsivity, emotional coldness and a willingness to manipulate others may help explain why these characteristics are associated with betrayal.

The conclusions come from a review of 11 studies examining dark personality traits and infidelity.

Participants included university students, married couples and adults from the general population.

All three traits were positively associated with infidelity, although the strength of the association varied between studies.

Psychopathic traits include impulsivity, low empathy and a lack of guilt.

Someone with these characteristics may be more drawn to immediate sexual rewards and less concerned about hurting a partner.

A willingness to take risks could also make the possibility of being caught less of a deterrent — impulsivity and deception may help explain this link.

Psychopathy had the largest average correlation with cheating, although its association was close to that of Machiavellianism.

Machiavellianism involves a cynical view of others and a willingness to manipulate people for personal advantage.

In romantic relationships, these characteristics could make deception easier to justify when it serves someone’s interests.

However, a calculating approach may also encourage caution.

Someone concerned with protecting their reputation might weigh the potential rewards of an affair against the consequences of discovery.

This calculated approach could help explain Machiavellianism’s slightly weaker link with cheating.

Narcissism involves feelings of superiority, entitlement and a strong desire for admiration.

Attention from another potential partner may appeal to someone who places great importance on being desirable.

Nevertheless, narcissism had the smallest average association with infidelity and produced a less consistent pattern across the reviewed studies.

An inflated ego alone therefore offers relatively little information about whether someone has been unfaithful.

The broader picture may depend on how personality combines with relationship satisfaction, commitment and access to alternative partners.

Dark traits provide only part of the explanation for why people betray a partner’s trust.

The study was published in the journal Psihologija (Ataman & Yalçınkaya Alkar, 2025).

A World Model to Predict What You’ll Look at Next

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the most frustrating aspects of using the old autoencoder-based FaceSwap program (or the more popular DeepFaceLab, which had exactly the same issue), was trying to get a person to either look to camera, or not look to camera:.

The IA Change Image tool is one of many, including functionality native to Photoshop in the neural filters section, that offers consumers a chance to rethink eye direction. Source.

If the training data for the personality did not have enough ‘eye contact’, camera-facing examples, the model trained from it simply did not have the data to generate that eyeline, since it had discounted the few to-camera examples as outliers in the training data, during the training process.

Conversely, if one had used ‘influencer’-style videos as the primary data source, it would be practically impossible to get the AI persona to not look at the camera, since ‘eye contact’ was dominant in the data.

You would think the age of diffusion-based generative AI would have ushered all these issues away; yet recognizing, changing, and predicting eye direction remains a very dark art even now.

In 2023 NVIDIA’s Broadcast app offered eyeline-changing on demand, though it did not seem on launch to be a reliable or totally convincing solution:.

Recent findings suggest that A grab from the premium demo for NVIDIA Broadcast’s gaze-altering functionality. Even in this flagship example, the AI-altered version does not really look to camera properly. Source.

Photoshop included a Change Eye Direction facility in one of its Neural Filters even before the advent of Firefly GenAI in the program; but neither of these methods have ever worked very well. Likewise, asking even the best of the current frontier Vision Language Models (VLMs) to subtly change eye direction in a photo still obtains spotty results.

Photoshop’s gaze correction feature relied initially on cloud processing, since most users lacked the GPU resources needed to perform the task locally. Even then, achieving a convincing change in gaze required considerable manual retouching. In both examples shown here, the original eye color has been poorly reproduced. In the Jennifer Lawrence example the iris is softly-rendered; in the Ryan Gosling example, the iris appears considerably smaller. Source  (The author’s own work at another domain).

Recent findings suggest that the problem is the very small amount of ‘action area’ involved in eye direction, both in the real world, and as a pixel-percentage of footage. Though I used to obtain some limited improvement in autoencoder-based genAI tools by specifically training eye-contact/averted paired datasets, that kind of approach is really pushing against the domain trends in the base model.

Diffusion-based models, unless diverted by ancillary mechanisms, tend to treat all sections of images and videos as equally important; one can therefore imagine the sheer volume of variegated eye data necessary in a training set to draw the model’s attention to such a small section of the total available image space.

A number of research methods have tried to improve on the state of the art in this regard by leveraging secondary indicators such as audio cues:.

Industry observers note that in the 2023 paper ‘Multi-Modal Gaze Following in Conversational Scenarios’ , audio is used as a clue to indicate eye gaze. Source.

Perhaps the most common and obvious proxy for gaze direction is head direction:.

It has been revealed that examples of head-based eye disposition guessing in a 2024 paper. Source.

But this presumption may be one of the main reasons for mis-prediction of gaze direction, since you never know when the owner of the eyes will be subverting it:.

Recent findings suggest that A case – albeit a telescoped one – where head direction does not equate to eye direction. Here the lateral diversion is very expressive, and indicative of some kind of narrative event, and clearly should not be dismissed as an outlier. Source.

Another recently-adopted proxy for gaze-estimation is evaluating what events are taking place in a scene, and guessing from that context where the eyes of an individual are likely to be alighting. For instance, this summer saw the release of the paper TextGaze: Prompting Gaze Target Estimation with Textual Scene Cues, which uses a VLM to generate textual descriptions of a person’s appearance, actions and apparent gaze direction, to establish where the person is looking:.

Test results comparing TextGaze (right) with the earlier GazeLLE system (center). The addition of contextual information helps the newer system locate gaze targets even when facial details are difficult to discern or other elements in the scene are visually distracting. Source.

As one can see from the examples above, in some of the cases under test, guessing the eye direction would even be momentarily challenging for us, even though (for reasons of mating and avoiding or sharpening combat) this skill is life-critical for humans.

Following on from this research is a more recent outing, a collaboration between the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and Google, titled Gaze World Model, which attempts to predict where a person will look next in a scene:.

It has been revealed that from the upcoming paper, test results using two clips from ‘It’s Always Sunny in Philadelphia’. Yellow boxes identify the people whose gaze is being tracked, green circles indicate where they actually look, and red crosses indicate the model’s estimates. The second and third frames in each sequence show future moments that the system had to predict without seeing the footage. Source.

Sources indicate that the system was trained on video sequences in which changes in people’s gaze could be associated with activity around them. The beginnings of a hand gesture, for instance, might be interpreted as an early indication of where another person’s attention will be directed.

Industry observers note that ‘Where a person looks indicates their focus of attention, and how their gaze shifts between targets reveals how that attention responds to a changing scene. Existing gaze target estimation methods largely operate frame by frame and do not model these shifts.

‘Gaze shifts are often driven by dynamic changes in the scene, which is the kind of information world models are designed to encode.’.

Industry observers note that with only two seconds of footage, the upcoming model allows gaze locations to be be predicted throughout the following second, with greater accuracy than was achieved by competing methods, the authors contend. In tests against both specialist gaze estimation systems and general-purpose AI models, including Google’s Gemini, nearly nine out of ten upcoming changes in gaze were successfully anticipated by the new system, compared to fewer than eight out of ten by its closest rival.

Recent findings suggest that GWM uses Meta’s V-JEPA 2.1 as a foundation. Unlike generative video models, V-JEPA was designed to learn how the physical world behaves from video footage, without having to reconstruct every pixel of a scene. Rather, its existing knowledge of movement and interaction was adapted to the specific task of gaze prediction.

According to recent reports, overview of the Gaze World Model. Current gaze is estimated from the available footage (blue), while future gaze is estimated from predicted changes in the scene (purple) from latent scene dynamics.

A shift in gaze was defined as a brief transition between two sustained periods of looking at different targets, as shown below:.

It has been revealed that illustration of a gaze shift from a person to an object. The subject (yellow dashed box) looks initially at the other person’s face before redirecting her attention to the sheet of paper. Minimum fixation periods and a maximum transition time are imposed to distinguish meaningful changes in attention from fleeting eye movements.

The three types of gaze shift studied were from one person to another; from a person to an object or other location; and from an object or other location to a person, based on the V-JEPA 2.1 methodology:.

Industry observers note that examples of V-JEPA 2.1 predicting upcoming human actions from first-person video footage. The colored boxes identify objects that the person may interact with next, with labels indicating the anticipated action and time until contact. Each set of predictions is shown alongside what actually occurred. Source.

Using the Scene-Head Interaction Module (SIM) from the earlier PaGE project, visual information about the person’s head was combined with information about the surrounding scene, and changes in both analyzed across successive frames.

Examples of zero-shot visual attention estimation from the PaGE study. Source.

Recent findings suggest that during training, greater weight was given to parts of the scene undergoing the most visual change, since these could contain early indications of events likely to attract the subject’s attention. Both the future location of the gaze and the likelihood of a shift in attention were estimated – but not the exact moment at which the shift would occur.

For training and evaluation, the existing VideoAttentionTarget and ChildPlay datasets were supplemented with annotations identifying changes in gaze.

According to recent reports, examples from the ChildPlay dataset. Source.

Through a semi-automated annotation process, 6,204 gaze shifts were confirmed, with 15,086 video segments used for training. For this purpose, Meta’s SAM 3 semantic segmentation model was used to identify people and objects at the annotated gaze locations, with temporal rules applied to identify potential gaze shifts.

According to recent reports, subsequently, Google’s Gemini 3.5 Flash examined sequences of frames to establish whether the subject had actually changed their focus of attention, rather than merely blinking or following a moving target. Ambiguous cases were referred to human reviewers, and random audits of 15% of the annotations conducted, with a final sampled error rate of 0.5%.

Tests were designed to evaluate how accurately Gaze World Model (GWM) could establish where and when a person redirected their gaze in existing footage – and predict gaze locations and shifts beyond the observed footage. Comparisons were made with specialist image- and video-based gaze estimation systems, gaze forecasting methods, and general-purpose multimodal models.

For gaze estimation in existing footage, GWM was tested against the image-based Gaze-LLE and PaGE systems, and MTGS, a video-based model designed to analyze social gaze. For the prediction of future gaze, the authors developed two implementations of the SAGE forecasting method (whose original code is unavailable) using the Sharingan Transformer architecture and PaGE to establish gaze locations.

Additionally, Qwen3.8 27B and Gemini 3.8 Flash were tested on both tasks, without additional training.

Training took place in two stages, initially using still images drawn primarily from the GazeFollow dataset, with additional material from VideoAttentionTarget, ChildPlay, and Multi-view Gaze Target Estimation (MVGT).

Recent findings suggest that the components trained to interpret individual images were then frozen, and the system trained on video sequences to anticipate changes in the scene and estimate gaze locations. Finally, these newly trained components were also frozen, and their outputs used to train the gaze-shift detection and forecasting modules.

Industry observers note that three sizes of the V-JEPA 2.1 visual encoder were used, frozen – ViT-B, ViT-L and ViT-g. Video clips comprised 16 frames sampled at 8fps, with gaze forecast for the subsequent eight frames. Training used four NVIDIA H100 GPUs, each with 80GB of VRAM.

Initial video training ran for 20 epochs with the AdamW optimizer, an effective batch size of 32, a peak learning rate of 0.0005, weight decay of 0.05, a linear warmup over 300 updates, and cosine decay to 0.0000001.

The gaze-shift modules were trained for 25 epochs using the same schedule, with a batch size of 64, a peak learning rate of 0.0003, and a warmup over 200 updates.

Sources indicate that test results for gaze estimation and gaze-shift detection in existing footage. The three variants of GWM (bottom) achieved the highest scores for detecting changes in gaze. Best results are in bold, and second-best results are underlined.

Recent findings suggest that in the tests, all three versions of the newly introduced model outperformed every rival at detecting changes in gaze within the observed footage, including the smallest version, with less than a tenth of the parameters of PaGE-H+. The largest version also matched or narrowly exceeded the best competing results in locating gaze targets.

About half of the improvement came from training the model to identify where a designated person in the scene was looking. The remaining gains came equally from tracking changes in gaze over time and predicting changes in the surrounding scene.

The two larger versions of GWM also tracked moving gaze targets more accurately than competing systems, with fewer fluctuations in estimated gaze locations, when the subject’s attention remained fixed.

Test results for predicting gaze locations and shifts up to one second ahead. The ‘Persistence’ baseline assumes that the last observed gaze location remains unchanged. Lower L2 scores indicate more accurate gaze predictions.

In a recent development, as shown above, the two larger versions of GWM outperformed all competing systems in predicting gaze locations, both half a second and a full second ahead, with gains of eight to ten percentage points in average precision for predicting gaze shifts. Compared to just extrapolating the last known gaze location, forecasting reduced average positional errors by 15.6% on VideoAttentionTarget and 11% on ChildPlay. Additional tests confirmed that accuracy deteriorated when the scene prediction component was removed*.

Recent findings suggest that it’s a testament to human acuity that a domain this small could be so dominant in survival, mating, and evaluation of all kinds in human life. Unfortunately, current trends in machine learning do not allow for an equivalent division and apportionment of attention when gathering and training a wider context of data, such as all-purpose image and video diffusion models.

According to recent reports, naturally, once you curate a face-only dataset, the eyes become a dominant feature and more can be achieved (though as I have noted, it remains an concern). However, it’s difficult to then apply lessons learned from that ‘close-up work’ to the wider context of integrated scenes, unless one plans to treat of the head separately – a clunky and Frankenstein-like proposition.

* We do not cover ablation studies, apart from exceptional cases, and therefore we refer the reader to the source paper for details of those.

Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1595 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral.
  • In a recent development, there are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team.
  • It has been revealed that mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral. It takes text and images as input and generates text. It has about 1T total, 49B active parameter, and a context window of 1M tokens.

The model is released in two official variants:.

In a recent development, there are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team. It’s distributed under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (an MIT derivative that establishes limitations for model-as-a-service offerings).

It has been revealed that mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality. In this post, we look at how the model works, its capabilities, architecture and more!

Mistral Large 4 combines a large pool of experts with sparse attention and a Pixtral vision encoder. The language model selects a small group of experts for each token, while its attention indexer selects which earlier token positions to attend to. These are two different forms of sparsity, where one selects feed-forward networks, the other selects context positions.

You can find all the checkpoints in the Mistral Large 4 collection.

Industry observers note that mistral Large 4 scores 82% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index test that asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch the software. Mistral reports that several closed frontier models score near zero on the same test because they refuse to attempt the work. This is super key for defenders, because fixing a vulnerability usually requires reproducing the vulnerability. In Mistral’s internal testing, Mistral Large 4 was also useful for malware analysis, vulnerability prioritisation and writing detection rules, which the model was not explicitly trained for.

Mistral mainly positions the model for defensive security work. Vulnerability research and incident response often appear like attacks in model input, so closed source filters can block them. A team that depends on an API can also lose access in the middle of an incident. Crucially, open weight models put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. That said, the model still declines harmful requests: on cyber prompts from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm, its average refusal rate is higher than any other open weight model.

For community builders, an open weight model like Mistral Large 4 unlocks a load of downstream use cases. You could build your own cyber system around your code base, crash logs, and malware samples. For example, with TRL you could fine-tune smaller models from Mistral Large 4 traces patching your code base. In fact, reproduce-then-patch tasks use a verifiable reward, so it fits with RL environments that could be used to further RL smaller security models. Open weights also let researchers measure the model’s refusal behaviour directly instead of relying on the provider’s description.

In short, cyber capabilities like ML4’s in the open are a huge boost for the community.

We have interviewed Pierre Stock about the cyber capabilities of the model, you can watch it here.

Sources indicate that mistral Large 4’s text decoder has 72 layers, a hidden dimension of 6,144, and 64 attention heads. Its attention blocks combine Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) with a DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) indexer (a direction in other models such as GLM 5.3). MLA keeps a compressed KV representation, and DSA selects up to 2,048 key positions for each query.

In a recent development, for each decoder block, there’s a 3:1 RoPE to NoPE pattern, i.e. 3 decoder layers employ RoPE and every fourth layer uses NoPE. The model also shares KV state across layers.The first decoder layer uses a dense feed-forward network. The other 71 layers use MoE blocks, in which a softmax router selects four of the 128 experts for each token. One shared expert always runs alongside the selected experts, for a total of 5 active experts per token.

Regarding RoPE, Mistral uses LeRope, a YaRN-scaled RoPE with one learned multiplier per frequency.

Recent findings suggest that mistral Large 4 employs a 1.6B Pixtral encoder. Pixtral has 30 layers, a hidden dimension of 2,048, and 16 attention heads. It uses 14 × 14 patches and a patch-merge projector with spatial merge size 2. You can see the encoder pipeline below.

Mistral Large 4 delivers strong benchmark performance across coding, cybersecurity, multimodal understanding, and agentic workflows, positioning it as a competitive addition to the open-weight ecosystem. As of October 29, 2026, the model is the fifth best open weights model on Artificial Analysis Intelligence index.

On coding, ML4 achieves 61.7% on DeepSWE v1.1, 59.4% on SWE-Atlas-QnA, and 28.3% on Terminal-Bench 4. Its combined Coding Agent Index score of 49.8% places it ahead of DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 and Qwen3.8 Max.

Coding capabilities of ML4 extend to knowledge work, with 59.9% on AutomationBench and 1,393 Elo on AA-Briefcase, which evaluate business workflows and long-horizon professional tasks.

Industry observers note that cybersecurity is one of Mistral Large 4’s standout capabilities, with strong results across real-world vulnerability assessment and security competition tasks. Three benchmarks highlight the model’s cyber performance:.

Mistral Large 4 also demonstrates 93.3% attack resistance on Lakera’s B3 benchmark, adding evidence of robustness against prompt-injection attacks. Beyond benchmarks, internal testing showed promising results in malware analysis, vulnerability prioritization, and detection-rule generation.

The Transformers implementation provides AutoModelForMultimodalLM, with AutoProcessor preparing the conversation and image inputs. Mistral Large 4 can take low, medium, high as reasoning effort. The default is high, and note that reasoning cannot be disabled, so using reasoning_effort: none would still use high.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, payer technology leaders are faced with AI sprawl – where system-embedded AI tools and third-party agentic AI platforms are promising faster audits, quicker decisions, and fewer manual interventions. The demos look impressive, but due to workflow integration and user adoption challenges, we find that core operations staff are still manually gathering context, interpreting policies, coordinating work across multiple systems, and pushing cases through the same queues.

The NAIC put US health insurers’ aggregate profit margin at just 0.4% in 2025. Administrative expenses, meanwhile, went up by $5.8 billion. Blue Cross Blue Shield Association research estimates that more intensive hospital coding practices, potentially linked to AI, may be associated with about $2.3 billion in additional healthcare spending. Hence, rising administrative spend, investments in legacy modernization initiatives, provider and regulatory mandates such as price transparency and electronic prior authorizations are pushing Payers to move towards faster, more transparent audit decisions and optimized core operations.

With these pressures mounting, Payer technology leaders must accelerate AI adoption and deliver measurable ROI within the next 6 to 8 months – without disrupting ongoing legacy modernization initiatives and ensuring regulatory compliance, including robust data security and governance across AI agents, knowledge, data, integration and platform layers.

Industry observers note that today many Payer operations rely on siloed and disintegrated legacy core platforms and monolithic applications. Claims data, benefit documents, contract clauses, and medical records often sit in separate applications. Every process requires many manual touchpoints for information handoff and validation. An audit analyst or frontline operator may have to open several screens, reconcile conflicting information, and chase missing documents before a case can move forward. Adding AI to one step may save some time, but it does not optimize the overall cost or turnaround time if the rest of the process stays fragmented.

However, replacing legacy systems and workflows may not be a financially viable approach for achieving short-term ROI.

An alternative approach is to enable AI-based coworkers that acts as virtual teammates to Payer operations staff and integrate with existing systems to gather relevant records, apply approved rules, identify missing information, and complete routine follow-ups. When an exception is found or there is a situation that needs human judgment, the AI coworkers can route the case to the right employee with the evidence and policy references attached. The key capabilities of an AI coworker are:.

Key Uses Cases: Audit Analyst (claims, prior authorization, FWA), Care Outreach Coworker, Member Services Coworker.

Sources indicate that auditors spend a fair amount of time just establishing whether a claim has been paid correctly. They need to check coding and benefits against provider contracts, while prior authorization reviews can get held up over missing documentation. Fraud, waste, and abuse (FWA) cases need detection of unusual billing patterns with perfectly legitimate explanation, but someone still has to examine the history behind it.

An AI coworker can pull together the relevant records into the review and flag likely overpayments with supporting evidence. Auditors then decide whether to pursue recovery or raise a dispute, while qualified specialists retain responsibility for clinical and fraud judgments.

A care manager calling a member may need to piece together information from several encounters to plan outreach or assign members to a CM/DM program. An AI coworker can take care of that preparation, leaving the manager with more time for the conversation itself.

It has been revealed that there are two potential financial benefits here. Care managers can reach more members without increasing staffing costs. Earlier engagement may also help lower medical spending, with care management programs showing fewer avoidable inpatient stays among members who engage early.

Member inquiries account for a regular part of a Payer’s operating costs. Even a seemingly simple question about whether a specialist visit is covered may require a representative to check network status in one system and benefits in another. If the information doesn’t match, the member may need to call again.

An AI coworker can pull the relevant policy and coverage details together while the representative is speaking to the member. More inquiries can then be resolved on the first call, reducing repeat contacts and the staff time spent handling them.

According to recent reports, the potential savings are clear in each of these examples. But there’s another cost to consider as Payers begin deploying AI coworkers across departments. A claims auditor and a member-services representative may both need access to the same benefit rules. If each team builds its own connections and maintains those rules independently, the Payer ends up duplicating the work and the expense.

Avoiding another layer of fragmented technology requires some decisions about how AI coworkers will be built, managed, and used across the organization.

Before committing to multiple deployments, Payer leaders need to work through six practical questions:.

To realize early value from AI, Payer technology leaders should not wait for broader enterprise AI platform enablement or legacy modernization initiatives to go-live. The pragmatic next step is to choose one high-volume, high-impact workflow and get started with an AI coworker model. Once initial, measurable value is delivered and proven, then reuse the capabilities built during the first 100 days to expand AI adoption in adjacent areas.

This approach will help the organization gain a clearer view of what AI costs and what it saves, and they can start reconsidering how technology and services are contracted. While contracting with vendors, fees linked to agreed outcomes can become a more realistic proposition. And if the savings from one deployment can help finance the next, AI investment becomes easier to sustain. Payers could gradually build an operating model where each latest coworker costs less to introduce, with more of the underlying capabilities already in place.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.
  • Today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research.
  • The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.

Today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research. ProtoStar brings together research institutions, industry, and the open science community to support the release of scientific artifacts in AI-ready, machine-actionable formats, and to demonstrate their value through a series of open challenges. The first challenge, hosted by Carnegie Mellon University, opens on November 2. See How to Participate below.

The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.

Participating organizations formalize their involvement through a memorandum of understanding supporting the release of suitable scientific datasets, models, and code in AI-ready formats on open infrastructure. Organizations interested in joining Project ProtoStar can reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

The U.S. federal government invests approximately $190 billion annually in research and development, and federal policy increasingly expects the results to be shared publicly. Agencies such as the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and National Science Foundation (NSF) have strengthened public-access requirements for funded research publications and require researchers to initiative for sharing the underlying data. Hugging Face is among the ten generalist repositories listed by NIH for sharing research data.

But making research publicly available does not automatically make it usable. Scientific datasets, models, and code are often scattered across incompatible systems, stored in static or legacy formats, or released without the documentation, metadata, and provenance needed to understand and reuse them. These limitations make it harder for researchers to build on existing work, and harder still for AI systems to discover, interpret, and combine scientific resources across disciplines.

Sources indicate that project ProtoStar aims to help close this gap by encouraging systematic sharing of publicly funded scientific artifacts in AI-ready formats, supported by open infrastructure and practical publishing guidance. It builds on efforts such as the National Cancer Institute's AI Data-Readiness Challenge and Hugging Face's guide to preparing public-sector data for AI. The goal is to make it easier for research organizations to meet existing public-access expectations while increasing the scientific value of the work they release.

The demand for reusable scientific resources is already evident. Hugging Face hosts more than 17,000 public datasets across core scientific domains, including genomics, protein design, chemistry, weather and climate, Earth observation, and astronomy. That figure approaches 29,000 when medicine and mathematics are included, alongside a comparable number of scientific models.

The pace of sharing is also accelerating. Researchers shared more than three times as many fresh science datasets on Hugging Face in the first nine months of 2026 as in the same period of 2025, with growth remaining substantial even after excluding the largest individual uploader.

Industry observers note that figure 1. New public science datasets on Hugging Face per quarter, by domain (Q1 2023–Q3 2026). Counts datasets still public, by creation date. Source: Hugging Face Hub data, October 2026. Explore the data.

When organizations share research in reusable formats, the scientific community can build on it at scale. The 18 public repositories maintained by NIH's National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) on Hugging Face have collectively received more than 11 million downloads, while NASA IMPACT's 27 repositories have received approximately 770,000 downloads, as of October 26, 2026. Documentation is also an important part of making these resources useful: 90% of dataset downloads on Hugging Face are from fully documented datasets.

According to recent reports, publicly available genomic data has proved important in contributing to research that further advances fields such as biological research; researchers at Hugging Face have been building on openly available scientific resources, including recent releases from HuggingFaceBio such as Carbon-A and Carbon-X. By releasing the resulting models, datasets, and tools openly, these efforts demonstrate how existing scientific resources can support new research that others can build upon.

This is the kind of activity that we are further catalyzing via Project ProtoStar through institutional policies adopted by participating orgs. As an early example of institutional commitment, CMU's Open Source Programs Office is encouraging its researchers to share suitable datasets, AI models, and other research outputs on Hugging Face, while recognizing the continued importance of domain-specific repositories.

Recent findings suggest that making scientific artifacts AI-ready is an notable first step. We also want to demonstrate what researchers, developers, and the broader scientific community can accomplish when those resources are made available for reuse.

A central question for ProtoStar is: Can publicly funded scientific datasets, models, and code, released in AI-ready formats, be readily discovered, reused, combined, and extended to accelerate scientific discovery and public benefit?

To explore this, ProtoStar will organize a series of open challenges, each hosted by a participating research institution and built around scientific resources that the institution has released openly. The challenges have two complementary goals:.

The resulting projects and lessons learned will help build a practical evidence base for making publicly funded science more accessible and useful.

Hosted by Carnegie Mellon University | November 2–13, 2026.

Recent findings suggest that the inaugural ProtoStar challenge invites participants to test whether AI can improve predictions of urban climate conditions using historical weather data from 210 U.S. cities. Building on research by Carnegie Mellon University, teams will use climate records through 2018 to predict actual conditions from 2019 to 2026, allowing their models to be evaluated against observed weather rather than hypothetical future scenarios.

Industry observers note that participants will forecast four indicators relevant to urban planning: average annual temperature, total annual precipitation, the hottest day of the year, and cooling degree days, a measure of demand for air conditioning. Their predictions will be compared against simple statistical baselines, including historical averages and linear trends, to assess whether AI approaches offer meaningful improvements in accuracy.

In a recent development, beyond forecasting, participants will also propose a short climate adaptation policy idea informed by what they learned from the data. This component encourages teams to connect scientific analysis with practical public benefits, such as preparing cities for extreme heat, improving energy efficiency, or managing changing precipitation patterns.

According to recent reports, teams will submit a Hugging Face dataset with these outputs. Forecasting performance will be assessed through a public leaderboard measuring prediction errors against established baselines, while policy ideas will receive separate consideration. Final forecasting results will be published in early 2027, once the complete 2026 weather records are available.

Explore the CMU Climate Risk Intelligence Challenge.

Recent findings suggest that the CMU challenge is the first in this series. Other participating institutions will host their own challenges sequentially, each highlighting different publicly funded scientific resources and opportunities for reuse. Future challenges will be confirmed through the Project ProtoStar page on Hugging Face.

Whether you're an academic researcher, student, independent developer, or company building on open scientific infrastructure, ProtoStar offers opportunities to put publicly funded research to work and help us learn what is needed to make AI-ready open science more widely useful.

We also welcome universities, federal research agencies, national laboratories, nonprofits, and other research organizations interested in making their scientific resources more accessible and reusable. To explore participation or collaboration, reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

Our hope is that ProtoStar will make it easier for publicly funded scientific work to reach the people and tools that can build on it, while generating practical evidence about the infrastructure and practices needed to support open science at scale.

Industry News: AI Literacy Is the Missing Layer of Deepfake Defense

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (992 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Detection tools are getting smarter, but most deepfake scams still work because the person on the other end didn’t know what to check.
  • In January 2024, a finance employee at Arup’s Hong Kong office received an email from the company’s UK-based chief financial officer asking for a confidential transaction.
  • It has been revealed that the incident is often quoted as proof of how convincing deepfakes have become.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Detection tools are getting smarter, but most deepfake scams still work because the person on the other end didn’t know what to check. That is a gap only awareness can close.

In January 2024, a finance employee at Arup’s Hong Kong office received an email from the company’s UK-based chief financial officer asking for a confidential transaction. He was suspicious. Then he was invited to a video call with the CFO and several colleagues he recognized. The faces looked right and the voices sounded right, so he went ahead. He made 15 transfers worth about $25.6 million. Every other person on that call was a deepfake.

It has been revealed that the incident is often quoted as proof of how convincing deepfakes have become. That is true. But one detail deserves more attention. The employee doubted the request at first. His instinct was working. What he didn’t have was the knowledge that a live group video call could be faked, or a clear rule on what to do when a request from the top feels wrong.

This is where most deepfake defense looks fall short. Companies are investing in detection software and platforms are adding labels, but very little is being done to help everyday customers understand what AI can do today. That understanding, or AI literacy, is the missing layer.

In a recent development, for years, the standard advice has been to look for giveaways – odd blinking, lips that don’t match the words, blurry edges around the face. These tips made sense when deepfakes were crude. They make much less sense now.

In a recent development, in 2025, identity verification firm iProov indicated 2,000 people in the UK and US a mix of real and AI-generated images and videos. Only 0.1% of them got every answer right, even though they had been told in advance to look out for fakes. Yet around 60% of the participants felt confident about their ability to tell the difference.

Low accuracy combined with high confidence is the real risk here. Teaching people a checklist of visual flaws may simply make them feel safer than they actually are.

Detection tools are improving, and they have an crucial role to play. However, they learn from yesterday’s fakes while upcoming generation tools keep arriving. Labels and watermarks help as well, but they can be removed. Moreover, many scams never pass through a platform that scans content. They arrive as a phone call, a voice note on a messaging app or a private video meeting.

Sources indicate that lawmakers are responding too. The TAKE IT DOWN Act, signed in May 2025, makes it a federal crime to publish non-consensual intimate images, including AI-generated ones, and gives platforms 48 hours to remove them once a victim reports them. Earlier, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) ruled that AI-generated voices in robocalls fall under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act, opening the door to fines and lawsuits. These are meaningful steps. But laws act after the harm is done. They can’t stop a cloned voice that calls you at midnight pretending to be a family member, and they can’t help you decide in that moment whether to trust it.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, the financial stakes keep rising. Deloitte estimates that generative AI could push fraud losses in the US to $40 billion by 2027, up from $12.3 billion in 2023. McAfee’s 2026 State of the Scamiverse report adds that Americans see an average of three deepfakes a day, and one in three have lost money to a scam, with an average loss of $1,160.

Sources indicate that scammers are targeting people’s trust and everyday habits. That is why our defense needs to reach people as well.

Sources indicate that AI literacy is often confused with knowing how to use chatbots or write prompts. When it comes to deepfakes, it means understanding three simple things:.

Recent findings suggest that the last point is the most overlooked. The Arup employee had the doubt. What he lacked was the permission and a process to act on it.

Building this awareness doesn’t require a massive budget. It requires consistency. Here’s where organizations can begin:.

Pro Tip: If a call or message asks you to act quickly and keep it a secret, treat that as the warning sign, however real the face or voice may seem.

According to recent reports, firewalls protect networks and detection tools scan files. AI literacy, on the other hand, goes wherever people go, whether it is a late-night phone call, a family group chat or a video meeting on a personal laptop. It is also one of the most affordable defenses an organization can build.

We have spent years teaching people not to click on suspicious links. Deepfakes need the same steady effort, with a upcoming message: what you see and hear online may not be real, and taking a minute to verify is simply good practice.

So, if someone on your team received a video call tomorrow from a senior leader asking for an urgent transfer, would they know it’s okay to hang up and call back?

According to recent reports, ragini Mittal is the Founder and Chief Vision Officer of EVERVELA, a practical education platform that helps people, families and organizations build confidence through everyday life skills, digital safety, technology and AI learning, and creative wellbeing. A technology and transformation leader with 18 years in heavily regulated industries, she has built enterprise AI governance frameworks aligned with the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, GDPR and the EU AI Act.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Just over a week ago, we released Granite Switch 4.1, showing that our modular Switch architecture lets you configure a language model with specialized, cache-efficient adapters — adding latest expertise on a single endpoint.

Granite Switch 4.1.1 is a patch release. The version number means what it means in software: fully backwards compatible with 4.1, no migration, incremental improvements under the hood.

While we are excited about these fresh features, what is notable is the speed and efficiency with which our teams could release this upgrade. Apart from training the new ASR model and Decision adapter, nothing was recomputed: the base model is untouched. You compose the latest adapters you want and deploy.

According to recent reports, this pattern can power far more than patch releases to an IBM-provided model. We're working on tutorials and an Adapter SDK so developers and third-party providers can build their own adapters — iterate on versions, test features, and ship updates the way you ship software. More soon.

Until then, test out our latest models, and try out the new multilingual and punctuation capabilities powering our Speech-to-Decisions demo.

#162276. Transformers Model Integration Contracts

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Transformers Model Integration Contracts

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1296 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that on July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5.
  • Sources indicate that when we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them.
  • Sources indicate that transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is major: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that on July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens. During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months.

Sources indicate that when we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built around it.

Sources indicate that transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is major: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention kernels.

Industry observers note that the integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a regression, it may already be in main.

Our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture: a small model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests" against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study, the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint is 1,227 MB.

This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU runners, but their fixtures run on CPU.

Industry observers note that model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-* checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5 bug would have passed a forward pass just fine.

Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a chance to catch bugs before they reach main.

It has been revealed that transformers-mic is a proposed standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has three parts:.

The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the baselines.

A contract covers an architecture and a usage path, not a single checkpoint: compatible checkpoints can share a fixture, while each keeps its own expected results. We publish them in huggingface-mic.

Sources indicate that for example, the SmolLM contract generates from prompts such as "The capital of France is" and compares its token IDs with a recorded answer. After loading the model and tokenizer, the generation code is, simplified to one prompt:.

It also compares training loss, checks that gradients are finite and verifies that an optimizer step changes the weights. See the full usage.md.

A fleet dataset on the Hub pins each MIC to a frozen revision, along with the package versions used to record its baselines. Each CI run records the fleet revision it used, so we can reproduce it later.

On a PR, we pick MICs based on the files the patch changes.

In a recent development, we replayed frozen MICs over five months of Transformers commits. The small UMT5 fixture flagged the regression from its introduction on July 30, 2026 until its fix on September 28. Label log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22 and training loss by about 0.20.

Sources indicate that one detail mattered: the contract used SDPA, the default attention path. Running only the eager attention variant missed the bug. A fixture only helps if it goes through the same code as the real checkpoint.

We then reverted the fix on a proof branch in Transformers' CI. The check failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup.

The replay results and the CI demo have the measurements and reproduction details.

Industry observers note that the first recipe was simple: make the dimensions smaller and keep fewer layers. That wasn't enough for mixed architectures. Keeping two layers is no use if both use sliding attention and the full-attention layers disappear.

We also keep the original weights file format. Otherwise we would skip the conversion code that runs when a user loads the real checkpoint. The full recipe has more detail.

The Llama 4 Scout shrink report shows what this looks like on a big model. 108.6 billion parameters become 44.7 million. The vision stack goes from 34 layers to 2 and the language stack from 48 to 4, keeping the checked layer kinds and MoE routing style.

Our CLI, tmic, creates the contract and builds the fixture. For a latest model, an LLM drafts the usage code and manifest, and CPU and GPU runs measure the candidate baselines. The LLM drafts; it doesn't approve. Changed expectations require human review.

To try it on your machine, use your source checkpoint in place of org/model:.

It drafts the contract, builds the fixture and records its baselines on your machine, asking you to review each step, and stops before uploading anything. For a fresh model, the draft comes from an LLM through Inference Providers, billed to your own account (--bill-to ''). The CLI docs cover the individual steps.

We used agents to build MICs across model families. When they hit an edge case, we fixed the recipe itself rather than the one fixture, with help from model experts. The published models and remaining gaps are in the coverage space.

Recent findings suggest that with random weights, our Whisper fixture barely responded to changes in the audio. It ran, but that made it a poor test of the audio path.

So we trained it on a few tones paired with words such as "red" and "green". We weren't teaching it speech recognition, just making audio changes visible in its outputs. In our weight-initialization study, the random Whisper fixtures caught 18 of 24 injected faults. The overfit fixtures caught all 24.

That gives us two ways to build the weights:.

The Whisper result doesn't settle which is better. Those were synthetic faults, and we haven't found a real regression caught only by the overfit version. Both versions missed an assisted-decoding bug that the real Whisper checkpoint exposed.

According to recent reports, so we keep random weights when they pass the checks, and overfit when we need better sensitivity or readable answers. Training takes seconds, but it is one more step that can fail to converge, and one more thing to maintain. The comparison has the results for both.

It has been revealed that as of November 1, 2026, the MIC job in Transformers CI reports failures without blocking PRs. Whether it should block depends on things we haven't measured yet:.

We also don't know how many bugs, like the Whisper assisted-decoding one, only show up with real weights, or whether overfitting catches real bugs that random weights miss.

According to recent reports, coverage is still partial, across model families and the APIs people use. When a regression slips through, we can add the missing usage path and replay it on the broken and fixed versions. We'll keep existing tests until their coverage is accounted for.

Finally, we'd like to link original Hub model pages to their MICs, so a developer or an agent using a checkpoint could start from an example tested on that checkpoint, its environment and its expected outputs.

Sources indicate that want to help? Pick an uncovered model from the coverage space, try the tmic workflow, and contribute a usage path or review a generated contract.

t5/umt5 in a blog post in 2026, never thought I’d see the day 😍.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that CWE-bench is designed to test the limits of frontier cyber capabilities.
  • A defender has to anticipate the ways an attacker could get in, and get it right every single time.
  • As part of our meticulous effort to keep improving quality, for every task we checked that the following questions were true:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that CWE-bench is designed to test the limits of frontier cyber capabilities. In our continued pursuit to push the horizon at Collinear AI, CWE-bench v2 opens up a public set of 100 tasks that anyone can run and evaluate their models on. The setup is the same as before. An agent gets a checkout of a real open-source repository and a short instruction, with the goal of finding and fixing a security weakness without breaking existing functionality. Scoring is fully programmatic, so results are deterministic and anyone can reproduce them without extra cost. All our programmatic checks have been curated with the help of LLM judge panels that shape them towards the direction of hardness and fairness. We also maintain a held-out set, so that we can keep tracking progress on tasks no model has seen. To evaluate your model on the held-out set, contact cyber@collinear.ai.

Our goal is to be exhaustive. A defender has to anticipate the ways an attacker could get in, and get it right every single time. These 100 tasks cover 91 different CWEs, spanning a wide range of vulnerability classes. A model that does well here has to understand the multiple weakness surfaces that a potential attacker can exploit. Recognising a familiar pattern is not enough.

As part of our meticulous effort to keep improving quality, for every task we checked that the following questions were true:.

It has been revealed that every task was also reviewed by hand. Open-sourcing the set is part of the same effort to improve quality. We welcome feedback on any task, and contributions to the public set.

In a recent development, results are tracked in two places on the Hub. The leaderboard on the CWE-bench dataset page covers open-weight models and updates on its own: labs and the community add a result by opening a PR on the model's repo with a results file (how). For the full comparison, including API-only models such as Gemini, Claude and GPT, see the CWE-bench leaderboard Space, where newly introduced models are added through a PR on the Space.

Open-weight models, from the dataset page:.

All evaluated models, including API-only ones:.

Of the 11 models evaluated, Gemini 4 Argon leads with 67.8% pass@1 and 81.0% pass@4, just ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (67.3% pass@1, 78.0% pass@4). 95 tasks are solved by at least one model, an indication that the tasks are indeed solvable. However, even the leader fails 19% of the set on every attempt, so the long tail is far from solved. The public set, the grader and the harness are open. Run your model, and tell us where it stands.

On cost, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (1017), Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon form the Pareto frontier: DeepSeek reaches 57.0% pass@1 at $0.04 per rollout, Opus adds ten points at $1.83, and Gemini edges ahead at $3.92.

According to recent reports, every task is a self-contained Harbor task (a Dockerized environment, an instruction, and a deterministic verifier), and the dataset ships a registry.json. Harbor can therefore run the whole benchmark straight from the Hugging Face repo, without cloning anything yourself:.

Industry observers note that -k 4 runs 4 attempts per task, and the reported score is the mean reward over all 400 trials. The dataset is gated: accept its access conditions on the dataset page first. Harbor fetches the tasks with git, so also save your HF token to git's credential helper once:.

The tasks are also tagged rl-environment: the same environments and verifiers can provide rewards for training defensive agents, not just for evaluating them.

#162266. Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language

📅 03 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1759 w)
